speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no occasion on the third reading to repeat the legal arguments which have been made in regard to section 27 of this bill. It is sufficient to re-emphasize that there is a wide difference of opinion as to the effect of section 27.
Perhaps it is sufficient to say that legal experts, whose field is directly related to this subject, have expressed the opinion that section 27 has the effect of completely reversing the application of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, in so far as the Canadian National Railways would be concerned if this section passes. I have conceded already, and I concede now, that legal arguments in regard to the application of a section of this kind are ultimately determined only by the courts. I do recognize that the minister has himself accepted the proposition that it is never safe to say with complete finality that a section of any act produces one result or another. There are too many decisions in our own courts and in the privy council which have upset emphatic declarations of that kind for anyone to be completely confident that his own interpretation must be the final and correct one.
Nevertheless there has been uncertainty. My own opinion is very definite that section 27 is both improper from the point of view of its legal application, and completely unnecessary. I do believe it is proper to point out again on the motion for third reading of the bill, which is for the purpose of consolidating a great many provisions relating to the Canadian National Railways, and which have nothing whatever to do with the purpose of this section, that there are other legal provisions which give the Canadian National Railways all the power it needs to operate motor vehicles of any kind.
I would point out again that the subsidiary company of the Canadian National Railways, set up for the purpose of operating motor vehicles, has, under its charter granted under the company laws of Canada, just as wide powers as has the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or any other railway company in Canada to operate motor vehicles.
I submit at this stage that there has not been one word which really justifies this addition under an act which is primarily for the purpose of consolidating general provisions of the Canadian National Railways Act. In fact, this section is an orphan among the general sections which are being consolidated. We agree entirely with the purpose of consolidation. We agree entirely with simplification of the numerous acts which are brought

together in this way. But section 27 is something new; it is outside the scope of these other sections. I repeat that section 27 is unnecessary.
Either there is some purpose not yet disclosed to this house for which section 27 is being introduced, or it has no weight at all. The subsidiary company has all the powers needed, and the Canadian National Railways now operate motor vehicles with the name "Canadian National Railways" on them. They are free to operate those vehicles in any way that might be desired, within any declarations made by the minister. I submit therefore that this section should not be included in this general consolidating act.
There is another point. Just over a year ago, at the time that the privy council had decided that all control over motor vehicle transport between provinces came exclusively under federal jurisdiction, this government invited representatives of the provincial governments to come to Ottawa to discuss that subject. Contrary to the decision which they had sought and had obtained from the privy council, they then invited the provinces to take full jurisdiction over the operation and supervision of motor vehicle transport of this kind. Since that was done a year ago, after the decision of the privy council, I submit it is appropriate, proper and in keeping with the right kind of relationship between this government and the governments of the provinces that the representatives of the provinces should now be invited here to discuss this and to indicate their opinions in regard to the application of section 27. Already statements have been made publicly that this section is questioned. All hon. members must be aware of it. That being so, it would avoid future disputes, future questioning and any uncertainty about the willingness of this government to abide by its implied undertakings to the provinces, if this section stands. If it does stand, no operation of the Canadian National Railways will be held back in any way. The consolidating section goes forward.
There is no appropriate resolution that can be introduced that would call for the government to invite the provinces. I am going to introduce a motion which will not have the effect of holding up the legislation, but it will ask that the bill go back to the committee of the whole house with the specific instructions that section 27 be deleted. Then the government could invite the provinces to have their appropriate legal representatives meet here to discuss the effect of the section, and if they saw fit they could then introduce this section separately later on in this session, if they thought it was 50433-311J
Canadian National Railways important, and have it dealt with in the light of the discussions which have taken place.
I would point out there is a special reason why there need be no delay. The representatives of the provincial governments are meeting here on Monday. It would be very easy for a telegram to go out this morning to all the provincial governments suggesting that they bring a legal adviser with them qualified to deal with this particular subject, if those who are coming here feel that they need any additional staff to deal with the question raised.
My motion is for the purpose of seeking the deletion of section 27, not to hold up the act. I recognize that I cannot make a motion which would give that specific instruction, but I want it clearly understood that along with the deletion of the section because of its legal application-that is, in my opinion and in the opinion of certain others-I also am making my motion with the express request that if it were accepted and, might I add, even if it is not accepted, the government immediately invite the provincial governments to bring any legal officials or other ministers they regard as appropriate to the meeting on Monday to have a separate meeting in some other room that could discuss this very subject while the other important subjects are under discussion on Monday and succeeding days that have already been announced.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
That Bill No. 351 be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions to amend the said bill by striking out section 27 thereof.

I think that is the fourth time the Leader of the Opposition has spoken of this bill as having an undisclosed purpose. All I can say is, and I say it for the fourth time following the example of the Leader of the Opposition, that there is no undisclosed purpose concerning clause 27 of the bill. I have said on four occasions-this will perhaps be the fifth-that the purpose of clause 27 is to enable the railway company itself, the parent company, and every railway company comprised in the national company, to exercise the power necessary to carry on delivery and pick-up services in the metropolitan centres, and to carry on bus or transport services in substitution for rail lines which are abandoned.
There is no undisclosed purpose. I think I have made that point abundantly clear on each occasion on which I have spoken in connection with this bill. It is not sufficient merely to say that Canadian National Railways may exercise these powers through its subsidiaries. I explained, I think on second reading, that particularly in the case of rail line abandonments it was the wish of the national company itself that it be in a position to operate bus and transport services where it is necessary to abandon rail lines, and to be in a position in proceedings before the board of transport commissioners to give in the name of the national company an undertaking to operate such services in lieu of rail lines being abandoned.
The second point is the concern which has been expressed by the Leader of the Opposition as to whether the Motor Vehicle Transport Act is going to be applicable to operations carried on by the national company or any other railway company forming part of the national company pursuant to clause 27 of the bill. It seems to me that the situation is perfectly clear. If the operations carried out are carried out wholly within the limits of a province, then it seems to me there is no doubt that the operations would be a local work or undertaking which under section 92 of the British North America Act, clause 10, falls within the limit of the legislative power of the provinces.
There is of course the exception contained in paragraph (a) of clause 10 of the section which speaks of interprovincial works, and I shall come to that in a moment. Then there is also the exception contained in paragraph (c), where works which are local and which are declared to be for the general advantage


of Canada would not fall within the jurisdiction of the provinces but would be under the jurisdiction of parliament. With respect to the exception in paragraph (c), I can only say that clause 18 of the bill makes it expressly and explicitly clear that any operations carried out under clause 27 would not be for the general advantage of Canada. It seems to me that it is abundantly clear that operations which are carried out wholly within a province therefore do not fall under paragraph (c), and if they are wholly within the limits of a province they must necessarily fall within provincial jurisdiction under section 92 of the British North America Act.
There remain the interprovincial operations which may be carried out by the C.N.R. under clause 27. I think it is perfectly clear that whether they be carried out by the C.N.R., by another railway company or by a company entirely outside the provisions of the bill, if they are interprovincial operations they will be subject to the provisions of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act.
Therefore the situation is this: Either the operation must be under provincial jurisdiction because it is carried out wholly within the province, or it must be interprovincial because it is carried out between points in two different provinces, in which case it would be subject to the jurisdiction which the provinces now have under the terms of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act. In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of referring the bill to the committee of the whole in order to delete clause 27 obviously fails. We have at all times said that we wished the operations under clause 27 to be carried out subject to the rights of the provinces and subject to their jurisdiction. It seems to me that we are effecting that under clauses 18 and 27 of the bill, and that no conference could add further to the bill or make it clearer that the rights of the provinces are being safeguarded in every respect.

speechtext:
I should like to hear the minister express his views on the very excellent suggestions presented to the house yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich as to the need for Canada's armed forces to be completely airborne. As they so clearly explained to the house, this is the only kind of force which would be capable of protecting Canada against the only kind of attack which could possibly be effective against this country, namely an airborne attack against our airfields or our key installations. To meet this kind of attack, troops would have to be moved to a danger area far more quickly than would be possible by conventional methods of transportation; and this makes our present formations which are not airborne, and which comprise the great majority of our army formations in Canada today, ineffective to defend this country against the kind of attack we could expect. In addition, as the Leader of the Opposition said, an airborne force of this kind would be the best possible kind of contribution we could make to our NATO allies.
What was suggested yesterday was that our forces should be made up of air-army combat teams, capable of moving on very short notice to any part of Canada to protect airfields and other key installations against apprehended attack, or to re-take those installations after attack has taken place.

The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich !Mr. Pearkes) described very correctly the kind of force we would need, as a fire brigade. I think that fits the description aptly, because an attack on Canada would be a very fast strike, and would require the kind of remedial treatment that a fire brigade applies to a fire-the ability to move immediately, and to go into action immediately upon arriving at the scene. I believe the establishment of men and equipment which would be necessary for these combat teams would have to be worked out carefully to obtain the best possible mobility and striking power.
Yesterday the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) very aptly suggested that we would need a great many more transport planes than are available today, or would be available under ordinary military planning. He suggested we should follow the procedure adopted in the United States, that of building many transport planes and leasing them out to air transport companies, with the understanding that they would be returned to the government in case of attack, and could be used to transport troops.
I believe these combat teams could be based upon a combination of an air transport wing, and an airborne battalion, together with the required supporting arms. I do not believe it is good enough simply to have airborne battalions capable of being transported by air, because in the kind of defence we will need here, the effectiveness of any defence force would depend upon the speed with which the force could be delivered to the required area. If there was the necessity to wait until the troops and their transport were linked together, after an alarm had been given, the purpose of the attack would have been achieved long before troops could arrive on the scene of action.
In order to ensure that we have the maximum speed of movement and effectiveness of action, I think we must work out a very high order of teamwork between the air force and the army well in advance of the time these components would be needed to work together. The time to start planning and working is right now. This kind of team work, which was worked out so effectively among the ground forces of the last war, at which time there were combat teams made up of components of armour and infantry working together, can only be accomplished if the air-army components train together constantly, work together, get to know each other, and almost live together. One could not expect that kind of teamwork if the air-army components were simply thrown together at the time they might be needed to repel an attack.
Supply-National Defence
These combat teams would not require the same kind of supporting arms as conventional formations do today. For instance, I believe that the artillery support which a force of this kind would receive would be provided by bombers and mortars, both heavy and light, in place of the conventional artillery pieces. Perhaps it might be found desirable to include a light tank in each of these combat teams, or perhaps light tanks. And of course supplies would be delivered by air instead of by conventional methods. If we go in for an airborne army, such as was suggested yesterday as being the most effective, we must reassess the needs of Canada and the needs of our armed forces, both as to manpower and equipment.
We have also to start thinking in terms of the air force and the army training together as combat teams, rather than as two separate services. Indeed, the government seemed to be on the way to working out this kind of operation between the air force and the army when it established three airborne battalions some time ago. The plan seems suddenly to have been laid aside, and I would be interested in hearing the minister tell us later why this has happened.
Another point I should like to discuss is the abrupt and premature termination of the services of the army chief of staff, General Simonds. In taking the action it did take, the government is, in effect, saying that General Simonds, at the very early age of 52 years, can give no further usefulness to our armed forces. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that the age of 52 is very young indeed for the retirement of a top executive-and the chief of staff in the army is just exactly that: a top executive. He works with his brains, not with his muscle.
I think it is important to remember that after the chief of staff has been retired for eight years, and has been drawing government pension for that length of time, he will then, and only then, be exactly the same age as the present Prime Minister when he decided to embark upon his present career in the service of his country. That was 13 years ago. I think the minister, and all hon. members, would agree that the Prime Minister is still pretty effective. And to consider that the army chief of staff, General Simonds, is ineffective at an age 21 years younger than the present Prime Minister, is, I suggest, somewhat ridiculous.
If General Simonds were just an ordinary soldier, his retirement might be understandable. But in my opinion he is the most outstanding soldier Canada has produced in many a long year. Those who had the privilege of serving under him during the last

Supply-National Defence war knew him as a brilliant strategist; and there is no one better able to judge the ability of a commander than the troops who serve under him, and who have to take the rap if he makes a mistake. In General Simonds, the troops who served with him felt that they were serving under a man whose judgment could be relied upon. When they went into battle following a plan he had devised, they felt they had the best chance of winning, and of survival. And that is very important to troops entering a campaign. It does much for their morale, as well as for the effectiveness of the force concerned.
General Simonds plan for the break-out from Caen to Falaise is conceded to be one of the most brilliant operations in the last war. To discharge this man of such ability at the age of 52 is, I suggest, an inexcusable waste of military ability, a waste of the kind of military ability our forces need today. General Simonds is, and always has been, a soldiers' general. I believe that he is far more capable than any other soldier in Canada today of leading Canadian forces into battle. His ability to prepare these forces for battle would be invaluable to this country for a number of years to come. I do say it is extremely regrettable that his services are to be completely discontinued from August 31. His services are being dispensed with because he simply refused to become a politicians' general and be willing to be a rubber stamp for the government's views in opposition to what he considers, from his very great experience, to be right. For that reason he has been cast aside at a time when his knowledge and his ability are at their very peak.
Another thing I want to speak about very briefly is the deplorable state of our civil defence. You have only to read the papers of the last few days to realize just how deplorable is the state of our civil defence, and also to know how seriously the United States takes this whole matter. We have all been very impressed by the civil defence operation carried out in the United States during the past three days. As hon. members know, the President, his cabinet, chiefs of staff, and all key personnel, were whisked away to some secret headquarters after the alarm had been given on Tuesday, and for the past three days they have conducted the affairs of that country just as though an atomic attack had taken place.
The President of the United States, his cabinet, the chiefs of staff, key officials and the people generally do not like to be moved about the country any more than anybody else does; but if they take this thing that
[Mr. Hees.l

seriously, it is important that we should consider doing exactly the same thing.
The President, by his action and by the serious way in which he has acted in this whole matter, is giving leadership in civil defence in the United States, and by this exercise that has taken place over the last three days, has demonstrated to the people of the United States that civil defence is an important defensive measure and one which must be taken seriously. If we followed that same principle here in Canada, people would stop taking civil defence as a joke, as they do today, and would start preparing under government leadership a proper plan to be used in case of an attack.

Mr. Chairman, if the mature members of the house would care to come back to their onions, I should like to get back to the question of defence estimates. Perhaps they are the most difficult of all estimates for hon. members to discuss, for two reasons of course. One is the heavy veil of secrecy that is thrown over the details of defence expenditures, a veil of secrecy that is excused on the ground of national security. Perhaps one might question at times the validity of that veil of secrecy when he contrasts it with the habits of every other government. However, there is of course a certain measure of secrecy that has to be imposed. Perhaps more important, hon. members are inhibited from discussing these estimates because of a feeling of, shall we say, incapacity, lack of technical knowledge with regard to those expenditures. But it does not excuse hon. members from their responsibilities. That is the trouble. We have to assume responsibility for those expenditures, and when they are of the colossal size of our present defence expenditures, then we have to do our best to discuss the nature of those disbursements.
Perhaps the first thing we have to get straight in our minds is just what we have in mind with regard to defence. It is a very wide and embracing term, and it sometimes creates in people's minds pictures that are not in accord with reality. If we were to decide where and in what form a possible attack on Canada might take place, then I think we have to eliminate from our thinking certain alleged possibilities.
Yesterday, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich was very sound in his suggestion that
Supply-National Defence in the final analysis the task of Canadian defence is defence against aerial attack over the north pole. We have to discard from any realistic thinking any possibility of an attack by ground forces on the area of Canada either by air or by sea. Anyone who has any knowledge of the terrain of the outlying parts of this country will realize that such an attempt would be worthless and useless and is not likely to be part of any aggressive plans which may be launched against Canada.
There is another thing we have to consider, namely, that any attack on Canada will be in essence part of an attack on the United States. I think we can accept that as virtually a fact; that an attack on Canada will be part of an attack on the United States. All of us have very clearly in our minds just what the nature of that attack might be. It would be an aerial attack on our industrial centres from the Arctic regions. We would have to discount the suggestion made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition of the possibility of airborne attack, for instance, on our uranium mines. I doubt whether that is a feasible possibility for an aggressor. I cannot see exactly what they would gain by such an attempt. Of course, the obvious suggestion is they would seize our sources of uranium; but of course they would be seizing the sources of supplies that would have to be used some considerable time in the future and would not in any way cripple, if that was their intent, the capacity of the United States and Canada at that immediate time. It seems to me that any sudden airborne attack would be merely part of a major aerial attack designed to destroy our existing industrial centres.
The next thing we have to consider is how well equipped we are to provide a defence against such an aerial attack. In the first place we have to examine the various types of military organizations which we have for that purpose. I am quite sure that the minister will agree with me when I suggest that ground forces of the army are of little consequence as defence from aerial attack. I notice that the Canadian Army Journal contains an article by the director of artillery at army headquarters here in Ottawa which has considerable bearing on this matter. I was interested in the comments made as to the limitations of conventional artillery. With regard to anti-aircraft guns he had this to say:
At a range of five miles, a fast plane will fly over two miles after the shell leaves the gun and before it arrives at the plane. Even if the aircraft does not deliberately change direction, very few pilots are sufficiently skilful to fly that distance accurately enough to be hit by a perfectly aimed shell.

Supply-National Defence Rather a sardonic way of placing the problem before us.
Therefore except at short times of projectile flight, predicted fire weapons do not provide a truly effective anti-aircraft defence against modern high-speed aircraft.
There are guided missiles in production now that can effectively engage manoeuvring, high-speed targets at far greater heights and ranges than conventional guns. They possess the capability of out-manoeuvring any planes that may be constructed.
That would seem to me to indicate that our conventional anti-aircraft defence would be of no particular value. I think we can wipe out the army on that score, with regard to that part of our defence. 1 imagine that the same argument applies to the navy. I do not think anyone will suggest that we could send an aircraft carrier to Baffin Land during the few weeks when the water would be navigable to shoot down approaching aircraft.
More serious are the statements by some outstanding military experts of the world which present us with a rather grim picture, one that apparently we are not yet ready to accept. I should like to quote from a speech made by Field Marshal Montgomery before the California Institute of Technology in November last year when he said:
There is at the present time no sure defence against the aeroplane or ballistic rocket. Indeed, so far as we can see today, trying to get a secure defence against air attack is rather like trying to keep the tide back on the seashore with a picket fence.
In addition to Field Marshal Montgomery we had a statement early this year by the famous Captain Liddell Hart, who has been military adviser to successive governments of Britain. He had this to say in January of this year:
Big savings could be made in ordinary bomber forces, navies and air defence, since none is capable of preventing "a catastrophic penetration by 'hydrogen bombers' or bombardment by atomic missiles."
Last year Sir John Slessor, chief of the air staff of Great Britain, gave two addresses over the B.B.C. which were later reported in the Listener, the organ of the British Broadcasting Corporation. Sir John pointed out that today it is not a question of stopping a percentage of attacking aircraft and wearing down the enemy by that means. He points out that because of the nature of modern bombs we would have to have virtually 100 per cent defence to have any effective defence at all.

The whole house listened with a great deal of attention, Mr. Chairman, to what we considered a statesmanlike speech by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I thought he gave a very complete outline of the situation and most constructive criticisms. We also listened with a great deal of interest to the presentation on behalf of this group by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to the constructive criticisms made by both these gentlemen.
It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to deal with the development of weapons and their use. I am a complete novice in that respect. The only weapons I am acquainted with, and have been over a very long period of years, are the mattock, the axe, the shovel and things of that sort, weapons with which you attack nature rather than human nature.
I am willing to leave the discussion of such questions to those who have knowledge in that field.
However, I wish to deal with two or three subjects which are directly related to the administration of the Department of National Defence and are of serious concern to many members of the house. Members do not express all their opinions in the house, but we have the opportunity to discuss matters with members of other parties, including members of the minister's party, and we know that many of them are quite as concerned about the matters I shall raise as are members of the opposition.
The first matter I want to deal with briefly is the necessity of maintaining the supremacy of parliament when it comes to the administration of the Department of National Defence. The second is our vigorous opposition, and I think I can include in that many members of the house, to any waste or unnecessary spending in the Department of National Defence. The third question-and I have had conversations about it with members

of all parties-is that we should make certain that justice is administered to all ranks in our armed forces regardless of their rank, background or prestige.
Before proceeding to deal with these three texts, which are the subject of my few humble remarks this morning, I want to pay tribute and give credit to the officers, warrant officers, non-commissioned officers and men of all three services and of the reserve forces who take their duties seriously and are playing an essential role in the defence of this country by giving their time and services for this purpose without any hope of receiving the feudal rewards that can result from a class and caste system.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, my first text is that the supremacy of parliament must be maintained. When dealing with this question, and particularly with matters relating to the army, I always have in mind the remarks of the late president Clemenceau of France who said on one occasion that war is too important a matter to be left in the hands of generals and admirals. I have remembered that remark throughout the years because I think it is a very great truth, and that is why we are so keen on the supremacy of parliament. In addition, it is possible that I am a little bit prejudiced as far as generals are concerned. I am not referring to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, for whom I have the greatest respect, and I am sure he will support many of my remarks. However, I may be a little prejudiced because of one or two unfortunate experiences I have had with generals in my brief military career.
I shall never forget-and I am quite sure the minister will know the person to whom I am referring-having to take part in a series of very heavy infantry attacks in the battle of the Somme in 1916 and, in the latter part of November, in snowy and bitterly cold weather, being fortified prior to the attack commencing with a ration of cold pea soup as the result of what most of us considered to be the pigheadedness of the general commanding our brigade who insisted that there was much more inspiration in cold pea soup prior to an attack than in the normal stimulant given to men who are facing rather unpleasant circumstances.

But in dealing with this question I do wish to refer briefly to several public statements made by senior officers prior to recent days which in my opinion indicate their lack of understanding-I hope their understanding has been developed as the result of events- of the fact that in a democracy parliament is supreme and only the government makes and announces policy. In that connection I want to remind members of the discussion of the Currie report and the consideration of that report by the committee on defence expenditure. I think all hon. members will recall that at that time General Guy Simonds published an article in the Canadian Army Journal of December, 1952, in which he said: In recent weeks and months the army has been the target of unremitting attacks from many sources.
The sources he was indicating are quite obvious.
We have been criticized for the indiscipline of Canadian soldiers. We have been criticized for too much discipline. We have been criticized for extravagance and criticized for not providing a whole host of things which cost a very great deal of money. We have been criticized for lack of morale and accused of complacency and arrogance when we have shown or proclaimed a pride in the Canadian army.
The general went on to say:
The Canadian army today is certainly not perfect and in several respects falls far short of the standards which I hope and believe we can attain. I have made our policies and objectives abundantly clear to general officers of commands and to commanders abroad.
Then he continued further:
Anyway, there were quite a number of people at that time who thought it was most improper for the

Supply-National Defence chief of the general staff to write an article which clearly implied a criticism of the persons who were criticizing a section of the administration of the Department of National Defence, and that criticism of course was largely concentrated in parliament and was coming from members of parliament.
I see that according to the Montreal Gazette, of Tuesday, January 18, the general made a speech. I might say this would not be tolerated in Great Britain for one moment. They have a very strong tradition in that respect. In any event, the general is speaking in Montreal and according to the Gazette he said:
"I would like to see every young man in Canada given two years military training." Lt.-Gen. Guy G. Simonds, chief of the general staff of the Canadian army, yesterday told the Canadian Club of Montreal.
"I have spent all my life in the army or in association with the army", General Simonds declared, "and I have yet to meet a man the worse for that association. A system of compulsory military training would be good for the boy, for the army and for the country."
Now, it is quite right for General Simonds to have these opinions, but it is quite improper for him to deal with the matter in a public address. It is definitely a matter of government policy and a matter of considerable debate and discussion in this country and upon which there is some cleavage of opinion.
Then, I see that according to the Gazette of the same date, General Simonds said:
"In any future war, however," General Simonds declared, "the United States will be in it from the beginning and will make a heavy demand on Atlantic communications. In two world wars, Canada was in for two years before the United States and had Atlantic communications almost to herself."

There again is a speech which gets very close to the field of policy.
There is an article in the Montreal Gazette of January 24 and I strongly suspect this was written by Mr. Blakely, who has no love for the ideas of the members of this group. I may say, therefore, I shall read it with greater relish.
Report is that Lt.-Gen. Guy Simonds, chief of the general staff, has been quietly cautioned to leave controversial defence policy references out of his public orations. Reason is his recent Montreal speech suggesting that it was high time Canada embarked on a policy of compulsory military service. The government defended the reference in public as having been a vague and harmless generality, but is anxious, it is said, to avoid a repetition. Parliaments are traditionally sensitive when military leaders enter the policy field. M.P.'s who agree with General Simonds' views on conscription are among those most critical of his public plunge into the controversy.

According to the newspapers I have read and public speeches by various people, General Simonds is given credit for three major accomplishments. The first is the present army form of organization, the army we have today; second, the organization of the Regiment of Canadian Guards; and third, the consummation of the small-bore arms agreement. I want to deal with those three accomplishments briefly.
In so far as the general's accomplishment in designing and organizing our present army is concerned, I cannot do better than quote the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. In his very interesting speech yesterday he had these comments to make. He said that Canada was maintaining yesterday's army to fight tomorrow's war. Then again I notice the hon. member, as an old army man himself, said that the army which regarded itself as time-honoured was really timeworn. He said that the army of today had changed very little from the army that fought on the Somme more than 35 years ago. I was under the same impression when I had a look at the weapons on display in the front of these buildings the other day, with the exception of the guided missile which I am told confidentially was a dummy made of wood.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich goes on to say that the whole army should

be an airborne army. Well, I do not know how this Regiment of Canadian Guards will do their goose step when they get into aeroplanes. Then he went on to say that this army was entirely unrealistic and there had been an entirely new concept of the army formation and role. I should say that I cannot quote any better authority than the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich.

No, I certainly regard the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, as a result of his experience and his mellowing experience in the House of Commons, which does have a beneficial effect on generals, as a good authority. In any event, I think it is safe to conclude from the observations made by the hon. member that our army organization is completely obsolete and as a result in recent years a great deal of the taxpayer's money has been wasted. That is the first accomplishment of General Simonds, the organization of an obsolete army which even the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich indicates should be reorganized on completely different lines.
I now turn to a favourite topic of some members in this house, some members of the armed forces, a good many members of the Canadian Legion and a good many people in this country, and that is the organization of the Regiment of Canadian Guards. The organization of this regiment has been criticized in the House of Commons, criticized in officers' messes, in military formations throughout this country, criticized in the Canadian Legion and criticized in public places everywhere. According to General Simonds there were two reasons for forming this regiment. The first was to give Canada a truly national regiment, as our other regiments had somewhat parochial connections. Well, their parochial connections did not prevent them from bringing credit to themselves when they were serving overseas in the defence of this country. The second reason was to glorify and glamourize the plain foot-slogging infantry. According to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, we do not want any foot-slogging infantry. We are going to have them riding around in aeroplanes. I do not believe, therefore, the arguments in favour of the formation of this regiment are very sound.
I was rather intrigued by an advertisement published by the Department of National Defence in an effort to secure recruits for the Regiment of Canadian Guards. I have some interest in this question because during a short period in the first world war I was attached to the guards, but I jolly well asked
Supply-National Defence to get back to my own unit as soon as possible. The advertisement reads as follows: Applications now being accepted for the new Regiment of Canadian Guards. Second to none on the parade square.
That is the place to which most of our generals relate their activities, the parade square.
Incorporating the colour and smartness of military tradition at its finest, the Canadian Guards ranks first among the army's regular infantry regiments.
Ranks first! Why, it was formed in 1953 and has fought a defensive rearguard action ever since.
Right now there is a requirement for young men who would like to share in the colourful dress and ceremonial activities of the new Canadian Guards.
Do you think the taxpayers of this country can afford to pay for the luxury of maintaining a regiment the principal purpose of which is colourful dress and ceremonial activities? Can we afford this, when already we have two regiments of guards in this country who have been active and performed many battle duties?
What do they do? Well, I will tell you what they are doing: They are trying to ape the British Brigade of Guards at Peta-wawa and that does not go down with Canadian society. If you go out to the parade ground you will find that their steps are being timed with a metronome and measured by a pace-stick so that they will maintain the exact distance of pace and number of paces per minute that is traditional with the number of paces per minute and the length of pace of the brigade of guards in Great Britain. I am just wondering how much this drill will assist in the defence of Canada.
Now, in our opinion, in the opinion of members of this group-and in this I am speaking for this group or, shall I say, on this occasion I am supported by members of this group-we find in this instance a return to the feudal conception. Do we want the glamour of uniforms and all that sort of thing, coupled with ceremonial drill? We suggest you would do better to leave that sort of thing to Hollywood. It is done better there, and people will pay to see it, but it is entirely out of place in the Canadian democracy.
We maintain, first, that it is a reflection on regiments in Canada which have rendered long service at home and abroad. It has caused a great deal of unnecessary friction in that respect. Second, it is a complete waste of public funds, as it serves no useful purpose in the defence of this country. And our feelings in this respect are heartened

Supply*-National Defence by the comments yesterday of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. Third, it is the breeding ground of class distinction, a military class system and snobbery. And we do not want any of these things in this country, in a Canadian democracy. Further, it is a complete waste of splendid Canadian manpower and material resources.
In the opinion of members of this group, ours should be a citizens' defence force, one composed of citizens who have offered their services to defend Canada on sea, land and in the air, without any thought of feudal rewards that are indicated in class distinction, in rank or in preference of position. Therefore we urge the minister to stop this waste of public funds. Listen to the plea of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich for reorganization, and in addition disband this unnecessary, inappropriate and most unpopular Regiment of Canadian Guards.
The third major accomplishment of General Simonds was the consummation of the smallbore arms agreement which, I understand, is to cost Canada, in the tooling process and purchasing of rifles, about $100 million. I suppose it is correct to say that there is a necessity for some small arms at this time. But I am wondering how essential a part small arms will play in an effective defence of this country.
Anyway, those are the three accomplishments of the chief of general staff. I want to be fair about General Simonds, because he is a man with a distinguished military record. But so often you find men who are successful under war conditions cannot become adjusted to civilian conditions, or those of peacetime. I think his opinion is rather well summed up by Mr. Austin Cross in the Financial Times of June 17. Let me say quite frankly I do not agree with Mr. Cross fully. In fact, about three issues ago he made some very caustic comments about me, all of which I take in my stride. But I understand that his whole family has a Liberal black-ground-

Anyway, Mr. Austin Cross has been snubbed and he takes it out in this article. He sums up his opinion when he says this:
Well, that's the end of gabby guys on parliament hill. The bouncing of chief of staff Guy Simonds sees the end of a gallant soldier but an insufferable civil servant. Surly, irascible, non-cooperative, I was glad I was able to duck anything to do with this fighting cock. Simonds retired after a period I regard as hopeless.
A brave man, he had no idea of how to get along with people. I would have written him off as a total loss were it not for my friend Leslie Mutch, the former MP, and soldier in two wars, whose opinions I value. Mutch had nothing but praise for Simonds and that to me is the only kind word I ever heard about this professional soldier.
A pro-conscriptionist; a fellow who was contemptuous of our politicians; a guy who could not care less about the taxpayers; Simonds would have made a great soldier in the German army.
He had courage, he had physique, he could do things, but in a peace loving country like Canada, he was lost.
He is succeeded by a fellow who is bound to be better, because he could hardly be worse, from my standpoint, at least. He is Major General Howard Graham, an amiable middle of the roader and a dark horse. We may perhaps return in army circles to the days when Charlie Foulkes, a gentle soul and effective soldier, was boss.
I might say General Foulkes is a very popular officer.
I have heard almost nothing of Graham but people here think he will be an excellent appointment.
However, I suppose you know why Simonds was told to move on. He too had made too much yakety-yak. Like his fellow Canadian Air Vice Marshal Plant, he was too loose with the lip on more than one occasion. Now he can fight the brave fight from our best clubs. There they can conscript to their hearts content over the whiskey and sodas, or if abstemious, over their cakes.
I do urge on behalf of this group that consideration be given to the disbanding of this Regiment of Canadian Guards, which has caused a great deal of criticism. When I say "disbanded" I do not mean a dismissal of the troops in question; they could be utilized along lines suggested by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. But let us stop all this unnecessary and wasteful expenditure which is now made for the development of ceremonial drill and glamour among the foot-slogging infantry, who are already disappearing from the scene.

speechtext:
What I wish to announce is that the government has appointed the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects which had been forecast by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) in his budget speech in April.
The chairman of the commission is to be Mr. Walter Gordon, of Toronto; and the other members will be Mr. Omer Lussier, of Quebec; Mr. A. E. Grauer, of Vancouver; Dr. Andrew Stewart, of Edmonton; and Dr. Raymond Gushue, of St. John's, Newfoundland.
The terms of reference of the commission direct it to examine and report upon Canada's economic prospects. In particular, it is directed to study developments in the supply of basic raw materials and energy sources, prospects for growth and change in domestic and external markets, the growth in the population of Canada, trends in productivity and living standards and prospective requirements for industrial and social capital.
Mr. D. V. LePan of the Department of External Affairs has been appointed secretary of the commission and director of research for it.
I should like to table copies of the order in council made this day, which contains the appointment of the commissioners and the terms of reference.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members will welcome the announcement as to the actual personnel of the commission. There are times when some people raise the suggestion that the appointment of commissions of this kind is an abridgement of the authority of parliament, but anyone who has studied the history of royal commissions of
Royal Commission on Canadian Economy this kind cannot possibly make such a statement with any expectation that it will be taken seriously.
In this particular case the chairman of the commission is a distinguished young Canadian who has won an enviable reputation for his objective approach to problems of this kind. He has in fact been called upon to perform similar services, not only for the government of Canada but for others. I am sure that he has left an impression of devotion and dedication to the task in hand which unquestionably commended him to the government in this case. The other members of the commission are men who will give broad representation of Canada.
I might simply add that in addition to the specific subjects which have been referred to by the Prime Minister-I should think the terms of reference are fully adequate for that purpose-I would hope that the commission in one branch of its inquiry would make an examination somewhat similar to that which was made in the United States as to the expected duration of the supplies of certain resources which are vital to our development. The recent findings in the United States in regard to their position in connection with resources came as a surprise to many people in that country and was something of a warning as to what can happen in regard to resources that seem to be plentiful and in no danger as to their possible continuity. I should think it would be extremely helpful if we had a clear and detailed analysis of the extent of our own resources and the expected life of those resources on the basis of any anticipated use.
I trust that this commission will lay the foundation for a fairly clear pattern in the future, but may I repeat that the findings of a commission of this kind are merely by way of assistance to those who must assume the responsibilities of government, and of course there can be no suggestion at any time that they infringe upon the full authority of parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank hon. members who have spoken. I can assure them that in selecting the members of this commission we had very much in mind the factors to which the Leader of the Opposition has referred. We tried to get a body of commissioners who would have special qualifications to deal with the broad aspects of the problem as a national problem and also with special knowledge of the geographical regions from which they have been selected.
As one indication, Mr. Lussier may not be as well known to all members of parliament as he is to me, but I know he has been called upon to report upon all the forests under private management in the province of Quebec. For some thirty years he has been most active in exploring the resources of eastern Canada and has pursued his studies for comparative purposes into the forestry undertakings of northern Europe.
Mr. Grauer from the west coast has been a keen student of developments in that whole area, on both sides of the Rocky mountain range. I am sure that hon. members from the plains know of the high qualifications of the president of the University of Alberta, Mr. Stewart. We have had experience here with the devotion to public duty of Mr. Gushue, who is the head of the Memorial College in Newfoundland and who has, in addition to his general qualifications, a special knowledge of the importance of fisheries to the economy of the Canadian nation.
As the Leader of the Opposition has said, no one need fear that there will be any undue influence exercised upon parliamentarians. There will be an objective report that parliamentarians will have to take the responsibility of using for the determination of policies that they feel best suited to encourage the continued development of this marvellously well-endowed land of the Canadian nation.

We share the high opinion of Lieutenant General Simonds that the minister has just now expressed. We feel that it is entirely unwarranted and far from the best traditions of this house that any member should get up

Supply-National Defence and attack a public servant of this government. General Simonds is not responsible for creating the brigade of guards. It was the government which formed the brigade of guards, and if there is any criticism-and criticism has been voiced on this side of the house-regarding the formation of this brigade, it is criticism directed to the government, not to the chief of the general staff.
While I am speaking of the guards regiment of Canada, I recall that my name was mentioned on several occasions in the speech made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. He said that I had urged the disbandment of that regiment. I did not urge the disbandment of that regiment but I suggested that, like the other units of the Canadian army, they should be reorganized and they should have an airborne role. Then the hon. member for Kootenay West began to ridicule the idea of guardsmen being airborne, and he cast slurs upon the tradition of the brigade of guards of the British army, a tradition which we in Canada share with the rest of the countries of the British commonwealth. I do not think it is necessary for me to elaborate upon the very glorious tradition in battle that the brigade of guards of the British army cherishes, dating back for several centuries. I would call attention to the fact that numerous regiments of the brigade of guards have rendered valuable service here in Canada and, in reference to the ridicule which was heaped upon these men when it was said that it was impossible for them to adopt modern conditions, I would call attention to the fact that the commander of the first airborne corps during the last war was Sir Frederick Browning.
I happen to have known General Browning for a number of years. It may interest the hon. member to know that General Browning started his service as an ensign in the Grenadier Guards in the first war. During the period between the first and second world wars General Browning commanded not only the King's Company of Guards but also the first battalion of the Grenadier Guards. When the second world war broke out he commanded the brigade of guards and from that command he was called by the war office to organize the first airborne brigade. He drew the personnel for the airborne brigade mainly from his own brigade of guards. From there, as the airborne forces expanded, he went on to command the first airborne division and finally the first airborne corps. I should like to put that on the record because I feel that an injustice has been done to a very gallant corps.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Macleod has asked me to dissociate this group completely in the course of my remarks from the remarks and the general attitude of the hon. member for Kootenay West in respect of General Guy Simonds, and also to express our intense disapproval of such remarks. I do not know what incentive there is for a man to strive upward through the ranks of the army, to do his duty and risk life, limb and health all the way, to assume the highest responsibility in the army with all that means, and to hold the highest post of honour for four years, if at the time he is removed from his position he is to be the object of such an unjustifiable attack as the one we heard this afternoon.
I want to be perfectly fair to the hon. member for Kootenay West. I know he has been in the army himself and has had a distinguished military career. If it were not for that, my words would be stronger still, but I cannot see how he could use such terms of contempt and ridicule and still not mean to express contempt and ridicule, because ordinarily the member is very accurate in his language and has no difficulty in expressing exactly what he means. I leave that point with the general observation that this country is not finished yet with the need for great military leaders. Every race in the world that has the sense it was born with is still prizing great military leaders and honouring them, and must continue so to do as long as the troublous times in which we are living continue.
Some of us have allowed all the talk about coexistence, peace and all that sort of thing to go to our heads. We had all better try to keep our feet on the ground, even those who are most ardent in support of this eternal peace, with Russia in charge of the world. That is what it amounts to. Apparently it does not matter a particle who rules the world so long as it is Russia and China. If we talk about the British being distinguished at all, that is "racism", but it is all right for

China to rule or Russia or the Mongolian outfit that are in charge of Russia. We will run right to them and kneel before them.
We have got to the point now where we do not dare speak up for the great, noble and wonderful Anglo-Saxon race of which we are a part and whose history has placed us in this house with all the advantages we have, has even given us this parliament, the flag, the Queen, the crown and the commonwealth. We have no time for that in the house, so much so that I am getting homesick for someone to get up and give a word of credit to the Anglo-Saxon race.
By that I do not mean to dissociate the splendid people from France who are joined with us in this country almost as if in a marriage relationship-and we are proud they are. We are proud of them. We want them to go along with us in unity and understanding, having inherited the great traditions of both their country and ours.
I wish to say one or two things along a line that more or less arises right out of what I have just said. I do not want to be critical of the minister, but I am not sure that the kind of thing being taught to our boys in the forces is the best thing for them. I have seen one or two pamphlets which were apparently part of a series being issued regularly in the forces. Those pamphlets were subtly poisonous through and through, subtly poisonous to everything that would make for the greatness of our race.
I know the minister will agree with me that in preparing for war we are preparing to defend ourselves against Karl Marx and the people who believe in Karl Marx. It is just as well to be frank about it. The Lenins and Manuilskys have said positively time and again that they will not stop until they have utterly destroyed capitalism. That means every one of the nations of the British commonwealth, and the United States. They have been working industriously and with astonishing success in the direction of the achievement of just that objective, and with the servile co-operation of far too many people in public life in Canada.
Before we finish the discussion of the minister's estimates I should like him to give the house an assurance with respect to the kind of thing that is being taught to our boys and girls in the forces. I want to know whether in the information that goes out through pamphlets and through lectures which they hear-heaven deliver them from a lecture by Brock Chisholm, for example- they are being taught to believe in God, to believe in the Bible, to believe in the Queen and the British flag. By that I do not mean what is called colonialism. I mean a reverence

I want to know whether they are taught to realize the importance of that flag.

Without any desire to hold up the debate, I should like to make one or two comments. I could not agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo this morning when, as I understood him, he suggested that our defence expenditures were entirely useless. I believe he quoted some American authority to suggest that with a proper air defence of North America it might be possible to shoot down up to 85 per cent of the attacking Russian planes, if and when such Russian planes ever attacked. Surely, with the destructive capacity which each plane would carry, it would be well worth while to shoot down even 85 per cent of the attacking Russian planes, assuming that 15 per cent of them did get through.
I agree with some hon. members when [DOT]they say that there is no real defence against the destructive devices of today. But after listening to some of the criticism in the last couple of days by hon. members opposite- and I exclude from this my very good and genial friend from Esquimalt-Saanich, whose masterly answer to the minister was I thought just as good as the minister's masterly presentation-after listening, as I say, to some of that criticism in which they suggested that all of our equipment is obsolete, and that we are thoroughly prepared for the last war instead of the next one, I must conclude that they are not in touch with the facts, ft seems to me that if this division which we now have concentrated in New Brunswick is there for a very good purpose, it is because it forms part of our obligation under the NATO treaty.
I should like to express one or two opinions on other matters. One is that no one has mentioned thus far in the debate the importance of the ground observer corps that has been so admirably built up all over northern Canada, in which tens of thousands of civilians are enlisted to detect enemy aircraft which cannot be detected by radar devices. Arrangements have already been made for the instant transmission of information to filter centres. I have seen some of the tests and I have been astonished by their efficiency.
So I believe that our defence, as it is now shaping up, is well worth while. I believe some hon. gentlemen opposite who suggest that all of the billions we are spending on defence have been utterly wasted would be the very first to complain if there were a Russian attack and if we had not managed to stop at least half those planes getting through.
The most ominous comment I have seen on what would happen in the event of an


attack was given by no less an authority than our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when, at the opening of the recent dominion-provincial conference, he said:
If a major war commences we cannot but expect at Its very beginning-that is, in the very first few hours-heavy attacks on North America with large nuclear weapons. These attacks would likely take place on Canadian targets as well as on those in the United States. The potential damage to Canadians and to the material fabric of our country in such event is so enormous that we must approach the whole problem of war and defence in the most deadly seriousness.
Now, without criticizing in any way the admirable reorganization of the forces that is now under way, and has been under way for some time past, I would like to suggest to the minister that perhaps some greater emphasis should be given in the future on the new type of training that will be necessary for our reserve units or militia units, as we now call them, in the light of the situation which would actually result in the event of a bombing attack. Because in the event of a Russian bombing attack there will be destruction of great Canadian cities. And I think we are living in a fool's paradise if we do not realize that fact.
Because of the terrible destruction that would take place in some Canadian centres at least-perhaps the most dangerous feature would be the aftermath-it would be necessary to move from their homes scores of thousands or even hundreds of thousands of people, some wounded and some suffering from the effects of nuclear attack. It would be necessary to move them, and the civil defence authority we have set up, or contemplate setting up, would be totally inadequate to deal with that particular situation unless our militia units were very carefully trained to take care of the situation which would then exist.
As I suggested a few months ago, Mr. Chairman, I believe the time has come when we must have a much more ambitious system of training for our reserve units in Canada than we have had in the past many years. In this connection, I should like to submit that if for any reason we have manpower problems that are not easily solved by the methods we have used in recent years, I for one hope we go back to the old fashioned militia act that was on the statute books of Canada for many scores of years. I believe that if, instead of adopting the type of conscription we tried to adopt in the first world war and the second world war, we had gone back to the old fashioned militia act, that was almost as old as this Dominion of Canada-actually older by that time-and was a combination of voluntary enlistment and selection by lot of the reinforcements necessary to bring militia units up to

strength, we would have avoided the great national tensions we had in both world wars. But in the light of the Prime Minister's statement, which certainly must be the last word in authenticity as to what would happen in this country in the very first hours of an attack, I for one believe much greater emphasis must be placed on the training of militia units to handle the potential chaos which might result immediately after the first bombing attack, and that we should take whatever steps are necessary in peacetime to see that we have a fully effective army to do that job.

Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied that the subject with which I propose to deal comes appropriately at this point. It arose out of a statement made by the minister last night just before the house rose. Therefore this affords me the first opportunity of dealing with something that goes to the very root of our whole method of organization. In Hansard for yesterday, at page 4913, the minister is reported as saying:
I should like to point out to hon. members that the first Canadian division is, of course, a division under NATO primarily for the defence of Europe.
Mr. Chairman, that is the first time that statement has been made. It is a statement of the utmost importance. It places clearly on record the fact that the first Canadian division is a division under NATO primarily for the defence of Europe.
The discussion yesterday hinged very largely on our proposal that we should get away from the old concept that the Canadian army in training, whether permanent or militia, is a segment of a European continental land force. We emphasized that because it had been pointed out by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that, in spite of changes in weapons, there has been a great similarity continuing through the first world war and the second world war in the unit formations. He pointed out that really today there is very little difference in the general structure of our army from that which was engaged in the great battles of the Somme or the other battles of the first world war and, later, the battles of the second world war.
In advocating, as I did, after it had already been put forward in very clear and understandable terms by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, that we should accept the proposition put forward in the white paper at the outset that there must be a new concept of Canada's military organization, we proposed that we should really bring about

Supply-National Defence sweeping changes in organization consistent with the inescapable fact that we have a population of only 15 million people in the third largest country in the world, a country of nearly 3J million square miles. We urged that the army continue to be made up of conventional units of infantry, artillery, armoured forces and other organizations of that kind. We urged, however, that these should get away from the continental concept of organization, and that we should have a unique, completely distinctive Canadian organization that would be suited to the demands here in Canada itself.
It was with that thought in mind that we proposed that all units be airborne. There is in fact no other way in which our units can be effective. I would point out that the hon. member for Vancouver South himself brought to our attention the attitude of the Prime Minister which, of course, must be the attitude of the government, that if a major war commences Canada will be involved in that war. If that is so, what is the use of training units which would be called upon to leave by road, by train, by boat, to travel long distances? The early, decisive stages would be passed before they would even become engaged with whatever enemy units had been employed.
The idea put forward that it would be unlikely that land forces would be employed by the only possible enemy we have in mind is not, of course, consistent with the history of recent wars, even of the last war. In the last war we saw cases of mass air attacks and at the same time airborne forces dropped at strategic points. In fact, at the time the Normandy invasion was taking place, key points were seized by paratroops-British, American and Canadian-who dropped from the skies to seize the strategic points well in advance of the actual movement of the conventional land forces. It is inevitable that, along with a mass air attack, there would be the use of paratroops to seize key points.
Can anyone with recognition of the importance of aluminum in military production be in any doubt for a moment that among the points in any Russian plan is the seizure of Kitimat, the seizure of Shipshaw and the surrounding plants, the seizure of the great iron mines at Sept lies, and the seizure of the various power plants through the northern area that supply the vital power to our industry?
It is obvious that this would happen. It is obvious that any employment of conventional troops in a conventional manner would be utterly ineffective. It is with that thought

in mind that we have urged that there be a bold reorganization of the Canadian army so that it may be completely mobile. We were urging that in the face of the premature statements by the minister, but we urge it with new force when the minister in his closing remarks last night for the very first time in this house or elsewhere laid down the policy of the government that our first division, our main army overseas, is a division under NATO primarily for the defence of Europe.
That is in conflict, Mr. Chairman, with every statement that has been made since it became necessary for Canada to revise its whole army concept after the outbreak of war in Korea. On February 5, 1951, when the discussion of the army was before the house for the first time that year, the then minister of national defence had this to say, after outlining Canada's program generally, as found at page 90 of Hansard:
That program is intended to provide, as Canada's part of an effective deterrent against aggression, what is considered necessary at this time for the defence of Canada against attack and to carry out Canada's undertakings under the charter of the United Nations and the North Atlantic treaty to the full.
That force at that time was of course entirely different from that which is now contemplated. Again at page 93 of Hansard for the same date we find this statement by the minister:
The defence plan for the first time set out particulars of the requirements for defence: it showed to what extent those requirements could be met; it also showed the allocations of forces that might be contributed by each of the member nations.
Then at page 94 we find this statement by the minister:
The force we propose to send will initially be a brigade group or regimental combat team . . .
That was the statement as to the force we were contributing under NATO. Then in the white paper for 1954-55, tabled last year, we find this statement on page 11 immediately after the word "army":
Since November, 1951, Canada has maintained a brigade group in Germany in fulfilment of Canada's commitment to the armies of the NATO integrated force in Europe.
May I emphasize the fact that last year's white paper not only emphasized that the brigade group was the fulfilment of Canada's commitment to the armies of NATO but that it was also our commitment to the integrated force in Europe. Then on May 20, 1954, the then minister of national defence, Mr. Claxton, had this to say as reported at page 4908 of Hansard:
So far we have carried out rotation in Korea and Germany exactly as planned, and we intend to continue to do so, but to do it will require very

considerable numbers of forces in Canada. Altogether, to provide for the brigade in Korea, the brigade in Germany and mobile striking forces and units for rotation forces with the forces necessary to make up a first Canadian infantry brigade, it will take a total of 15 infantry regiments. Those regiments now exist and they are well up to strength. They are well officered and well manned.
Then we come to the white paper for the present year and we find in the very first words of that white paper under the heading "Defence Objectives" this statement:
Canada's defence program continues to be planned for the immediate defence of Canada, for co-operation with the United States in the joint defence of the Canada-United States region, for co-operation within the North Atlantic treaty organization looking towards the provision of a collective force capable of deterring aggression, and for carrying out undertakings by Canada as a member of the United Nations Organization.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the statement of our defence objectives in the white paper. There is no suggestion that there is a commitment of a division, no suggestion that our primary purpose with the army is the defence of Europe as part of the NATO commitment. On the contrary, the very first statement is that our defence program contemplates the immediate defence of Canada and, in fact, the last of the several purposes declared is the fulfilment of our part in the joint undertakings of the United Nations.
The statement now made presents an entirely new picture, inconsistent with statements that have been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister. It will be recalled that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was questioned in the house after his return from Lisbon, where there was a meeting of NATO as to whether there had been any additional commitment beyond the brigade, and it was emphatically stated that no additional commitment existed. After the Paris meeting, which paved the way for the entry of Germany into the fellowship of the free western nations organized within NATO, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked if this involved any additional commitment for Canada, and he stated that there was no additional commitment. That statement, of course, was not made here because we were not sitting at that time. It was made in an interview.
We have constantly been impressed with the fact, Mr. Chairman, that there have been no commitments in addition to the commitment to provide a brigade as part of the NATO organization. Now we are told in the exact words of the Minister of National Defence that the first Canadian division is of course a division under NATO primarily for the defence of Europe. That is exactly the point we have been seeking to emphasize.
Supply-National Defence We need an explanation regarding the real function and purpose lying behind the training of our army. We have emphasized our belief that the army organization should be a distinctly Canadian organization, and that it should conform to the statement made in this year's white paper to the effect that the first purpose of the Canadian defence forces is the immediate defence of Canada.
What we contend is that the kind of organization that will be able to take part in the immediate defence of Canada in case of an attack is, in the case of the army, an organization made up of compact, hardhitting, mobile groups, all of which can be moved immediately by air to any threatened point, whether it be a hydroelectric power station, a mine where vital minerals are being produced, a harbour, or any of the key positions which would naturally be in any plan now in the possession of the Russian general staff.
I do submit, Mr. Chairman, that before we proceed with any detailed discussion regarding the army we should have a clarification of that point. I submit that it would be a very useful and, in fact, a very necessary thing for the Prime Minister himself to clarify this point, because if the statement of the minister last night was correct then we have assumed obligations of which no honourable member of the house was aware. We need to know exactly what our obligations are, and we repeat our request that our army shall not be trained merely as a segment of European continental forces but that, having regard to the fact that the first demand of our training should be the immediate defence of Canada, we should have a distinctly Canadian army organization suitable to the needs of Canada in the event that an attack should ever come.
We have said and we repeat that such a mobile, hard-hitting, compact army organization would not only be an effective organization for the defence of Canada in the unhappy event of any outbreak of this kind, but would also be the most valuable contribution we could make to NATO itself, because it would be the kind of force that we could move to any danger spot anywhere in the world as part of our general commitment to NATO.
I leave the subject there, in the hope that not only the Minister of National Defence but also the Prime Minister may clarify the uncertainties which have now been created by the Minister of National Defence through his declaration for the first time in the house that we have a commitment of one division as part of our NATO obligation for the defence of Europe.

As everyone knows there is being opened in New Brunswick, Gagetown camp, the largest military camp in the dominion.
