I might say we hope and feel that this camp will be a great success in our province. We wish all those troops who come to New Brunswick at


this time, and in the years to come, an enjoyable stay with us and very profitable training.
I was a little surprised when Gagetown was selected a few years ago as the training area. It was one of the best farm sections in New Brunswick, a very old, settled part of the province. I had always advocated and pressed for a training camp in New Brunswick. At that time I felt it should have been in some other section. People have been moved out of that area, some 1,100 families or over 3,000 people in all. I believe they have been moved to other parts of New Brunswick and other parts of Canada, and now they are fairly well settled. As I say, I do hope that this camp, for the sake of the people of New Brunswick and for the sake of Canada, will be a great success.
I agree with my leader and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that today our army must be trained as a mobile unit. In training these men as a mobile unit, it would seem to me that this camp, particularly as a new camp and the largest in this dominion, should have airfields associated with it. I should like to point out to the minister, and I hope he will give it consideration, that in the vicinity of Camp Gagetown there is an airfield known as Blissville. It belongs to the Canadian government, and it seems to me that for the training of the men at Gagetown that airfield should be developed. At the moment it is not used and the buildings and runways have deteriorated. It does seem like a great waste of money, if the field could be used to a good purpose. Also not more than about 25 miles away there is Pennfield, another airfield which belongs to the Canadian government. I believe that in the future those airfields should be used in conjunction with the development at Camp Gagetown.
When the camp was being discussed for New Brunswick I thought Utopia in the vicinity of Pennfield was an area which would be selected. It was near the sea, and it had this airfield belonging to the government nearby. There was a great area of land in the rear which was clear, and it would not have been necessary to take over land which had been settled. However, the Department of National Defence in its wisdom decided to take the Gagetown area. I hope these matters I have mentioned, Pennfield and Blissville, will be given consideration by the government because I believe these airfields would be complementary to a modern camp such as Gagetown must be.
While I do not wish to advertise our severe winters in New Brunswick, I must say that we do have some winter weather. However, the winters in any part of Canada are

severe and they are no more severe there, possibly not as severe as here in Ottawa where the temperature goes many degrees below zero. I hope Gagetown will be used for the training of men in winter exercises. It can be done there just as well as in the areas farther north. I see the Minister of Defence Production in his seat. While this might not have to do altogether with national defence, we have in that area of New Brunswick supplies which could be used for national defence. We have a splendid farming area in the country surrounding this camp. It is a small fruit growing area, and the apples and other fruits could be used. I hope this will be done. I was pleased to hear that coal, which comes also from the area in which this camp is located, is to be used in heating Camp Gage-town.
I might say to the minister that we are pleased with the development of what is practically a small city in what is known as Oromocto. However, I pointed out in the house before, and I would point out again, that those who suffer most from the establishment of this camp at Gagetown are the people along the fringe of the Saint John river, between the camp and the river. I do not think all the construction should be in one area, that is at Oromocto, just below Fredericton. As I say, these other places have suffered most from the establishment of the camp. While

Mr. Chairman, in the few remarks I make this afternoon I wish to discuss a line of defence which has not been dealt with up to this time. The history of man, the rise and fall of nations, can be traced to their ability to adapt themselves to changing weapons of war and destruction.


Today we have reached an age when for 10 years we have had atomic and nuclear weapons. Thus man's ability to destroy himself has developed so rapidly that we are having difficulty in keeping pace with the modern weapons, some of which are obsolete by the time they come off the production line.
This is one of the problems facing us today. As we look at the expenditures of the Department of National Defence in 1955 we wonder how long a nation can go on spending money in this fashion, how long it can use its national production and its power to produce things which very soon become obsolete and have to be discarded. I wonder whether the cost may not ultimately break us, or whether a war would not annihilate us.
The duty of members of parliament is to investigate and question the expenditure of money which the government is spending in its administration, and this is one of the important departments. The amounts spent on defence today are almost as great as those spent by all the other departments of government put together. On page 57 of the white paper we are given some figures which will astound a good many people, and which would have been thought impossible a few years ago. On the navy we are spending some $290 million; on the army some $346 million; on the air force some $923 million. On mutual aid we spent some $320 million, but we get some of that back in refunds. Then on administration and pensions we spent another $48 million. We cannot be given the full details of all of the expenditures for security reasons. Probably that has to be accepted. Someone has pointed out that this is why it is difficult for members of parliament effectively to question and give adequate consideration to all the details of these expenditures.
The minister's statements at the beginning of this debate were rather interesting. We welcomed his frank statement with regard to the effectiveness of our defence expenditures. His statement was that there is no 100 per cent defence against thermonuclear attack if it should be launched against Canada. That was the reason we had to go in with such groups as NATO. It is rather significant also to learn that it is folly for people to talk in 1955 about winning any war. All mankind would lose if war were to break out today. Therefore our best defence is our ability to deter such an attack.
How long are we to continue in this race? How long are we going to be able to continue in it? I suppose time will tell, but I do think one thing might be said. In this fight our ability to find out what modern warfare can

do and what we can do to deter the opposition is largely a matter of what research can do. To be up to date in modern research is surely one branch of national defence which should be emphasized. If we are to continue in this race we must continue research. Canada's ability in research has been well proven in years past, particularly in time of war. If a real assessment of the efficiency of the department were made, and some of the facts looked at with regard to the ability of industry to produce weapons which will be up to date at the time they are delivered, compared with what we might be spending in research, we might be surprised. I suggest that production research is very important.
There was a change-over in the use of Canadian small arms and ammunition. That change-over at this time might be questionable. We might even question the effectiveness in a war of the future of certain types of rifles, artillery, machine guns, certain types of depth charges, anti-aircraft ammunition and so forth. What can nations produce in the way of modern weapons which would be effective in a nuclear war? Let us look at the situation in a broad way. Perhaps the people of the world are going to have to look for other ways of preventing war, other ways of meeting what we believe is the enemy today.
I wonder whether we are doing our part in looking forward to the real fight, which is a fight for the minds of men. Research and studies under the United Nations, the Colombo plan and the food and agriculture organization reveal that about a billion people in the world are living in hunger and poverty, disease and malnutrition. These are the people who are being won over by the enemy with respect to whom we are spending this money on defence.
I wonder whether there is not another line of defence. Should we not be spending more money than we are spending today to win these people over to the democratic way of life? If we can spend almost $2 billion a year, which was more than the whole annual wartime expenditure in the first world war, on this kind of defence, I wonder whether we might not be doing well to spend money to win these people to the democratic way of life, to show them that democracy has something more to offer to the world than hoarding up our own abundance. Surely if there are a billion people in the world who need assistance, food and human compassion, we cannot say that there are any such things as food surpluses.
If we spent a few hundred million dollars to provide these people with food, with 50433-313
Supply-National Defence assistance and with education as to the importance of sanitation, training them how to use the land and the resources they have, might it not be an action of broader vision than some of the waste which I believe must exist in the defence program as we have it today? That food and assistance might be a more effective weapon than all the weapons we can produce.
Ten years ago atomic bombs were dropped by our allies on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and monuments have been erected on the spot where those bombs fell. The simple message that has been placed on that spot is the hope that mankind might never again be guilty of dropping an atomic bomb. With respect to dropping atomic bombs on mankind, the thought we might throw out to governments today, not only here but elsewhere, is that which has been expressed in the United Nations, namely that no nation can win a war. The possibility in going along the road we are travelling is that mankind may be annihilated if war, which we hope to deter, breaks out. If that should happen, half of mankind would be wiped out.
If we are trying to win the war for the minds of the peoples of the world, to show them that democracy has something to offer other than $2 billion a year spent on modern warfare, I humbly suggest to the government that the spending of a few hundred millions of dollars on bread, assistance and human compassion for the free people who are being won over to the other side would do a great deal more good.
I am looking at it from the point of view that this government might think of the possibility of another line of defence. The government should look upon these fellow men of ours, a billion of them, who are living in want today, as people who might be won over to our side. If we can win them to our side in a real way perhaps this defence race, which is costing us so much and leading us we know not where, might be terminated successfully.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is any real ground for misunderstanding about our commitment. The phrase I used

Supply-National Defence may have been an unhappy one, but it was accurate. The record shows that the 1st division is for NATO defence purposes. That is not new and it is not secret. I shall possibly be able to explain the meaning of it a little later. At page 9 of the annual report of the department for 1953-54 under the heading "NATO" we find the following:
As a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Canada continued to assign components of the three fighting services for duties with NATO forces. In addition, substantial quantities of mutual aid were given by Canada to other member nations. Highlights of Canada's role in fulfilment of her NATO obligations were the formation of the 1st Canadian infantry division with headquarters at Petawawa, Ontario.
Then again at page 41 of the same annual report, the second paragraph under the heading "Formations Abroad" reads in part:
During the latter part of 1953 the 1st Canadian infantry division was formed in accordance with our NATO commitments.
And on page 16 of the white paper which was tabled this year on June 7, we find the following in paragraph 53:
Towards the end of 1953 and in accordance with our NATO commitment, the 1st Canadian infantry division was formed with headquarters in Canada. Two-thirds of the division are stationed in Canada and conduct their training here; the remaining third, the 1st Canadian infantry brigade, proceeded to Germany and relieved the 27th brigade there in November, 1953.
I am somewhat at a loss to understand the difficulty of the Leader of the Opposition. I think the facts of the practical application of these commitments are and always have been understood to be that our commitment in peacetime is to have a brigade group across the Atlantic as part of the integrated force under SACEUR. That was the case at the outset and I think my predecessor explained it on a number of occasions; in fact the Leader of the Opposition quoted him to that effect.
Rotation forces are needed. The brigade proceeds to Europe and remains for a two-year tour of duty. Then it must be replaced by a duplicate brigade organized and trained to fit into the SACEUR forces before departure from Canada. For this reason forces required for NATO must be kept separate.
For the defence of Canada we have the mobile striking force of three airborne parachute-trained battalions. These are the forces which would be utilized in the event of any engagement with the enemy which might take place in Canada. I might say in addition that we are committed, as are other nations in NATO, to pool our resources and work together for mutual safety and protection.
As I mentioned, of the battalions which make up the 1st division all but one brigade
[Mr. Campney.l

are located in Canada and are here if needed. In order to keep a brigade continually in Europe in peacetime, and yet allow the personnel a reasonable period at home in Canada, we must have further brigades for rotation.
There has been a great deal of discussion-the Leader of the Opposition initiated it and the hon. member for Calgary North and other members referred to it-that our Canadian forces should all be airborne. While that may sound rather attractive I must say that I am of the view, on the advice of my military advisers, that, having regard to the long distance we are from our potential enemy and the fact that any men landed here would be far from any bases, the likelihood of invasion by persons in numbers has decreased, as the power of the bomb, which would otherwise be carried by these longdistance planes from far away, has increased. It is felt, and I am so advised, that the three battalions which comprise the mobile striking force are adequate protection for that type of warfare should it arise.
To have troops airborne is an expensive matter. I made a rapid calculation this afternoon of what it would cost. One element of cost is the aeroplanes necessary to move the division, to make the division airborne. I think as good a transport aircraft as we could expect to have is the C-124, which can lift 120 men, but without anything except their personal arms. To lift a division of 20,000 men would take 175 of these aeroplanes which cost approximately $2 million each. If you wanted to move the division in one lift, you would have to have $350 million worth of planes, plus the cost of the planes needed to carry equipment, plus the cost of the more expensive planes needed to carry tanks, artillery and that sort of thing.
The other side of the picture would be this. If you did have a great number of airborne troops, more than you needed, where would you take them? What is the purpose? I think what we have meets the situation as it is both with regard to our NATO defences in Europe, to which we contribute, and the defence of Canada, which is our responsibility.

Mr. Chairman, if it would be more convenient to deal with this particular subject now there are some comments I should like to make, but if the minister would prefer to deal with other points there are certain comments I should like to make in regard to what he has just said.
I had hoped that my own remarks, to say nothing of what I thought were the extremely clear remarks of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Calgary North, had made it clear that we were talking about an entirely new type of army; we were talking about the use of conventional forces reorganized into much more compact, hard-hitting and mobile units. At no time was any suggestion made by us that the present massive form of our division would be simply taken up bodily as it is now formed and moved by air. An examination of what we said makes it perfectly clear that that is the very opposite to what we were suggesting. We are suggesting a unique Canadian army organization. It would involve a smaller number of men of higher hitting power and of immense mobility.
May I again also point out that the remarks the minister has made are no answer to the comments that have been made about the statement he made last night. I would point out that it is only today that we have had a chance to deal with this, because this is the very first time it has been put on the record. It is true that reference was made before to the fact that there was the formation of a division so we could take our part in the NATO activities. It was also clearly stated that our commitment was one brigade for the defence of Europe, and it was explained in 50433-313i
Supply-National Defence this house and outside the house that we required the division so we could maintain the brigade with the rotation mentioned in the quotation I have put on the record from the speech in the House of Commons by the former minister of national defence.
What the minister said last night was that the 1st Canadian division is, of course, a division under NATO primarily for the defence of Europe. That means that the whole division is under NATO; and it also means, if the words mean anything, that it is primarily for the defence of Europe. The minister has said that the troops here are primarily for the defence of Canada. They cannot be primarily for two different purposes. If the statement of the minister last night is what he really means, then this is a new statement. If the minister wants to say that in the course of the debate last night he made a statement that did not correctly put the facts before us, that would be a different thing. But if he stands by the statement made last night, then we have had for the first time in this house the statement that our division is a division under the control of NATO, and these are his words: "primarily for the defence of Europe".
That is his statement. Unless he withdraws that statement it is obvious that we need not one division but at least three divisions in Canada if we are to carry forward the same general practice. We would need a division available for the defence of Europe and two divisions available for the purpose of rotation, consistent with the plans that have already been made. That, of course, would be an entirely new concept of army organization, an entirely new demand, that would involve figures that go far beyond any suggestion we have made.
I state most emphatically that the proposal we have made for a reorganization of the army forces into airborne units embracing not merely airborne battalions, but airborne units of artillery, of armour, of medical services, of army service corps, of every other component branch of the army, would be much less costly than the present cumbersome type of division which is simply a segment of a European army.
On that basis I have been asking, and other members have been asking, for a Canadian army formation equal to the Canadian demand. We point out that the kind of force that is suitable for the Canadian demands, immediately mobile, ready to be put into action within a comparatively few hours at any point in Canada, is also the kind of force that would be most valuable to NATO, because it could be moved within a matter of 24 or 36 hours to almost any threatened point in the world.

Instead of that the present organization can only be assembled slowly, then moved slowly and ultimately carried to some destination by ship. That is not the kind of force suitable for the defence of Canada, nor the kind of force that will make the most effective contribution to the joint demands of all the members of NATO.
I ask the minister to explain to us what he did mean by the statement he made last night or else explain that-as all of us must reasonably do from time to time-in the exchange of debate a statement has been made which did not correctly convey what he meant to say. Unless he is prepared to state that, we have a new statement, and one which demands close attention.

speechtext:

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE Defence services-
236. To provide for the Canadian forces, the defence research board and other expenditures relating to defence, including contributions toward the military costs of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization; to authorize expenditures in the current year out of the amount hereby provided, not exceeding $175,000,000, under the provisions of section 3 of the Defence Appropriation Act, 1950, and to provide that, notwithstanding subsection (3) of that section, where equipment or supplies acquired by the Canadian forces after March 31, 1950, are transferred, the estimated present value thereof shall, if the governor in council so directs, be credited to this vote instead of being paid into the special account mentioned in the said subsection (3), and when so credited may be expended for the purposes of the Canadian forces; and notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act to authorize total commitments for the foregoing purposes of $4,269,726,540 regardless of the year in which such commitments will come in course of payment (of which it is estimated that $2,443,441,346 will come due for payment in future years), $1,729,285,194.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Calgary North reiterated today a number of requests which he made last night. He asked a number of general questions which I do not think can be dealt with easily in the form that they were asked. They have already been dealt with in a general way which is about the only way you can deal with them.
He asked what is our defence policy, what is the disposition of our troops, and how did we arrive at the figure of 120,000 as a ceiling of manpower. As to the number of personnel, all I can say is that it was felt that 120,000 personnel were sufficient to discharge our present tasks. If new tasks arise or present ones are extended or decreased the ceilings will again have to be considered. They are not permanent. They have been
Supply-National Defence changed a number of times, but they represent our best judgment as to the number of personnel required for the duties we have laid out.
As to where we will get new men if we need more men for the air force-and the hon. member says he thinks we will-these are problems I am not going to try to decide here and now. If they should arise they will be dealt with to the best of our ability and judgment.
I have noted the observations of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre on the break-down of the estimates. I am not too familiar with the history of this matter, but I have a feeling that they were set up in this way to conform with the desires of the Department of Finance or some branch thereof, so they might be systematically arranged like the other estimates. I think that is the reason they were changed some years ago, but I may be wrong.
I wish to thank the hon. member for Vancouver South for his reference to the ground observer corps. Because of the number of matters to which I had to refer yesterday I did not have time to make reference to it. The ground observer corps stretches across Canada now and consists of about 80,000 civilian volunteers at 5,000 posts and with 12 filter stations. We feel it is performing very useful work. I should like to say that we are most appreciative of the number of people who have come forward to volunteer and who are actually following up and taking part in this very useful service.
I think that about covers the points that have been raised today, and if hon. members agree perhaps we could now proceed with the details of the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I am by no means satisfied that the questions I asked have been answered. The minister has brushed them aside as being of a general nature and has said they cannot be answered any more than they have been answered. I do not think that is the case. One definite thing he did tell us yesterday about the infantry division has, I think, clarified our defence policy to some extent, particularly in view of the further explanation he has made today.
I believe what I have asked is quite reasonable and simple. I have asked that we be given further clarification regarding the role of the other elements in our defence forces, and particularly that we should be told-1 have already asked this twice-what changes in emphasis are taking place. It is indicated in the white paper that changes in emphasis are under way. What are those changes? I think the minister should be able to tell us

Supply-National Defence what changes are contemplated if they are not already in being. I believe we are entitled to that answer, and the minister should be able to give it to us.
In connection with the ceiling of 120,000 as the maximum number of persons in the regular forces, we have had that figure now for some considerable time. It was not arrived at just this year. We have had it for the last two years at least, and I think longer than that. In spite of the fact that we have had that figure for this length of time, we now find that very considerable changes are taking place in the general organization of the forces and in the emphasis to be placed on the roles of the different arms. That is why I asked what relationship the figure of 120,000 bears to defence needs now as compared with three years ago. Three years ago the Korean war was on. It is not on now. I think the minister could give a much more definite answer than he has given.
Then there is another matter. We now have in the forces some 3,000-odd women whom we did not have a few years ago when we also had a figure of 120,000 as the maximum. What proportion of the 120,000 in the regular forces are going to be women? Is it planned to have 5,000, 10,000, 15,000 women in the forces, or merely another thousand or two? I think that is a definite part of defence policy as far as manpower is concerned, and we should know.
As I say, I should like the minister to be a little more definite with respect to the figure of 120,000. He said he could not say how it had been arrived at, except on the advice of his military advisers. If they advised 120,000 three years ago, surely they are not still advising the same number in the light of changing conditions. There must be some other explanation unless, as I said last night and as it appears to me, it is a purely arbitrary figure.
With respect to the role of the 4th brigade, in answer to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich I understood the minister to say that as far as he knew it was for reinforcement purposes. That is no role at all. Surely the brigade has some other role than to serve as reinforcements. If that is the only role it has surely it is an extremely bad thing for the morale of the brigade. If I were in the brigade and knew that the only role I had was that of reinforcement I would not be too interested in the development of the brigade, no matter what my position was. I would think I was only going to be there temporarily and was going to be sent some place else 

as a reinforcement. Why would I be interested in building up unit spirit, a good platoon, a good company, a good battalion or whatever it might be?
I could not imagine any statement which would be worse for the morale of that brigade than the one the minister has made, to the effect that its chief role is to provide reinforcements and so forth. As a matter of fact I hope that brigade is going to be continued, and it should perhaps be trained in the same way as the airborne brigade is trained. The people in it should be given airborne training, and perhaps some of them should receive parachute training and others training in landing aircraft. Certainly I would say that the present situation is very unsatisfactory. In any event, I think it must have some more definite role than just reinforcement. I would think that for the welfare of that brigade the minister should perhaps correct that statement.
I do not think I have been unreasonable in asking the minister to give more definite answers than he has given concerning this change in emphasis in so far as the role of the various air force units is concerned, particularly in view of the fact that the number of these home defence squadrons equipped with the CF-100 is going to be increased to nine and the role of the auxiliary fighter squadron is to be reassessed.

I think if the hon. member would look carefully at my statement yesterday he would find that I developed to some extent the question of reassessment. If he will compare the figures of the units and the forces, he will see there is a changing emphasis from the army, for example, to the air force. I was only making an observation about trends. There is nothing permanent about the figure of 120,000. There have been some variations in the figure and it may have to be varied again.
As regards the auxiliary air forces, I think I said very frankly yesterday all that could be said about the matter at the moment. In view of the nature of modern planes, heavier planes and more intricately equipped planes, the role of the auxiliary air force is being reassessed to see how its services can best be utilized. Our air defence might have to be reviewed and revised as a consequence, but I do not propose to try to spell out every change in detail. I do not think I should be expected to do that. There is nothing static about these things. They change with changing conditions, as they are bound to change. As I say, general questions of this nature are not easy to answer in specific terms. I do

not think that is an unreasonable answer to what my hon. friend referred to as a not unreasonable question.

I would point out that one of the difficulties with which we are confronted is the very large group of figures embraced in this single item 236, calling for a total expenditure of $1,729,285,194.
The second point with which the minister has not yet dealt, and one which has an important place in these general items, is the training of the militia. Will the minister indicate to us whether any change is going to be made to give effective training to the militia at these great camps we have established? I dealt with one particular type of training, the artillery training. We have great camps, wonderfully equipped, suited for the training of artillery units, yet the fact is that this year, which we are told is such an important year from the defence point of view, only a fraction of the artillery units are going to go to camp.
In addition to that, no plans have been made for competitive firing or other competitions or other activities in Canada as they were in the past. Will the minister tell us something about what the prospects are of getting back to a really effective form of militia training in our camps?

I have been informed on a number of occasions that the reorganization of the militia, which has been proceeding during the past year, and which includes the artillery and the other arms of the service, has progressed steadily, including training activities. I am surprised at what the hon. member has said. I am told the training is better, more use is being made of equipment and that generally the whole training of the militia is being conducted in such a way as to improve the activities of these services. I have been informed that a good deal of progress has been made in the past year in improving the training.

I can only express more than surprise, I can only express amazement if the minister is surprised at the statement I have made. All he needs to do is obtain a list from the officials concerned of the number of artillery units in Canada and the number that will actually be carrying out firing practice at the camps this year.
I am obtaining them.

If the minister has that he will find that only a fraction of the units in Canada will actually be carrying out firing practice. I have used the artillery as an illustration because I happen to know something about it
Supply-National Defence from personal contact. The fact is that without firing practice artillery training is largely useless. Any suggestion that at this time we have militia forces that could be used in the event of an emergency would be completely remote from the facts. I can only express my admiration for the men who are carrying on under the difficulties they encounter.
When this huge sum of money is being spent, we are not getting results from the units in our reserve forces. I think before passing on from this item, which embraces all the training items of this kind, we should have some explanation, not only in regard to the artillery but in regard to armour, the engineers and the other services. We should be told what percentage of the men actually enrolled in local units are going to get training in camps this summer. Hon. members are wholly unable to even express an effective opinion in regard to the adequacy of our training methods unless they know that simple fact.
Carried.

It cannot be carried until we have some indication as to what is contemplated from the point of view of training. Surely the minister can, possibly within a few minutes, obtain a statement of the units of infantry, artillery, the armoured forces and the other services, with the number of men enlisted and the number of men from those services that are going to camp this year. Those figures are now available because plans are made. Can the minister get that for us?
I shall endeavour to do so. I do not think I can get the full information for all the different services within a few minutes, but I shall endeavour to get what the hon. member wants.

I should like the minister to tell us about plans for the training of the militia. After all, it has been represented to us over and over again that the militia is the backbone of our defence training. Can the minister tell us exactly what the plans are for the training of our militia, and to give them the kind of training at camp that will at least to some extent prepare them for any possible emergency they might be called upon to face?

I am certainly not in a position to give the details of the training schedules of all the services at this time. I think the Leader of the Opposition is rather unfair in suggesting that. The training officers of each of these branches have organized their training plans, and I have discussed them generally with them. But I have not any detailed knowledge as to how many people

Supply-National Defence are going to these camps, for what periods they are going, or the details of the training syllabus. I do not think I should be expected to have such material here. I shall get what the Leader of the Opposition wants; but most certainly I do not have it with me.

Mr. Chairman, let us just see exactly where this leads us. The minister suggests it is unfair that we should ask him to tell us the percentage of men on the strength of the militia units who will get camp training this year. We have great camps in this country, camps on which millions and millions of dollars have been spent. Not far from here is one of the greatest artillery camps in the world, at Petawawa. That camp is capable of training every artillery unit in eastern Canada and of taking the fullest establishment permitted for training.
Surely the minister should be able to tell us what the relationship will be between the number of artillery units in eastern Canada that are actually active, and the number of those units which will take men to camp this summer. Anything less than that would make our discussion of militia estimates a farce. Surely that is the basic information we require.
That camp is for the purpose of training artillerymen. We have a great infantry camp at Gagetown, and other camps for infantry and other branches of the service. We have camps at Shilo and Valcartier and camps farther west across Canada, all created at great expense.
Surely the first information we should have before we can express an understandable opinion as to the adequacy or otherwise of the preparations being made by the Department of National Defence in regard to what is considered as the backbone of our whole defence system is to be told how many infantry units, how many artillery units, how many armoured units, how many engineering units and how many units of other kinds there will be.
If the minister tells us he cannot give us that information now, then perhaps he will say that at a later date or at a later point in the discussion, when the officials of his department are here, he could give it to us. Can the minister assure us that this will be done?
Yes, certainly.
Then we may count upon having the officials present when the militia estimates are dealt with?
The officials who are usually here will be here.

I know that; but I am pointing out that this is basic information. Will the minister give us the assurance that there will be officials here who can give us information in regard to the number of units of the various services actually-to use the army term now being used-activated, and the number of men from that enrolment who will be at camp this year?

I shall undertake to get
the information. That is all I can say.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Without taking
part in the debate, may I point out to the committee that item 236 for $1,729,285,194 is, in the details, broken down into five major headings, namely departmental administration, navy, army, air and research. If by consent we proceed to the discussion of those five major headings, one at a time, thus permitting questions and answers, by proceeding with that discussion in that way we are not in any way approving or carrying item 236. As I understand it we are just enabling the minister to have before him the proper group of officials to deal with each subheading. Then when the discussion is finally concluded it will then be necessary for the Chair to go back and put item 236 to the committee.

If it is done in that way it will be entirely satisfactory. I had understood from an earlier statement that you did not feel it should be done that way. However, if this is done we can proceed with the details under those headings, and then deal with the single item.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Then I would point out to the committee that the details are to be found at page 306, and that the first heading is that of departmental administration.

Under this heading I see there is no great change in the amount. The civil staff has gone up, and that was to be expected. But we had always questioned, from this side of the house, the necessity of employing a large number of professional and special services. I note with some concern that while the amount in this particular item is not so large, there has been an increase in professional and special services from $25,000 to $35,000. In view of the large number of professional men in the various services, can the minister explain why it has been necessary to engage this outside assistance?

The major item in this increase is for the services of a consulting engineer in connection with planning for new accommodation for the department. He has been engaged to work on that project. The

remainder erf the item is $25,000, the same as it was last year, for the bureau of current affairs.
I note at page 307 that the department has listed a librarian, grade 3, and a librarian, grade 1. Do the requirements for those positions necessitate the holding of a degree in library science?
I cannot answer categorically, but I am reasonably satisfied the answer is no.

I note at page 306 an item for a real estate appraiser. What are his duties? Does he go out to all parts of Canada appraising the value of real estate the department is considering purchasing or leasing?
I understand most of our appraisal work is done by local people in the areas where we are operating. This man is the co-ordinator of their efforts.

I note that while the salary of the deputy minister was $15,000 last year, it is $20,000 this year. I am not making any implications, nor am I suggesting that the present deputy minister is not worth that much. As a matter of fact I take this opportunity to pay tribute to him for the work he has done in the Department of National Defence. We read in the press that in a short time he will be leaving the department to engage in a different occupation. I believe he has great gifts and has exercised them with energy in the post of deputy minister.
I rise, however, to point out this increase from $15,000 to $20,000. Looking through the estimates I find different amounts in different departments. While in the Department of Finance and the Department of Justice the deputy ministers are to receive this year this same amount of $20,000, in the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Agriculture they receive $17,500, in the Department of Fisheries the amount is $15,500, and in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources it is $15,000. Then in one branch of the Department of National Revenue the deputy minister is to receive $15,000 and in the other branch $16,500.
How were these increases arrived at, and why is there this very considerable variation?

The salaries of the deputy ministers and of other senior officials are approved by the government. They are based on the recommendations of the treasury board after a very exhaustive study, and they have recommended varying rates.

This is a change. They used to be all the same.
Supply-National Defence
Ever since I have been familiar with the matter there have been changes from time to time, and the salaries were at varying rates some years ago.

There is another matter in this particular detail. I notice on page 307 the total personnel under departmental administration last year was 769, and this year it is 791. There is a small increase; but when we turn to page 30 of the white paper, where there is a break-down of civilian employees at national defence headquarters, we find that instead of these figures of 791 this year and 769 the year before the figures of 756 and 647. What is the explanation of those figures? Which figure is actually correct?

The figures in the blue book are the number on the establishment. The figures in the white book are the actual number of personnel. In other words, some of the positions on the establishment were not filled last year; some of them are not filled now.
The minister estimated for them last year and he is estimating for them again this year, in spite of the fact that the positions are not filled?

I understand they are not always the same positions that are not filled, but generally speaking it has been the history of the establishment of the department over some years that it normally runs somewhat below the actual numbers of the establishment as fixed.

In this instance there is a difference of 124 out of a total of 769, as far as last year was concerned. That is shown in the blue book. In the white paper only 647 are shown. Surely there were not 120-odd positions in this group which were not filled.

I see that the establishment last year was 769 and the actual positions filled were 756, which is a difference of 13. We have not the final figures for this year to put against the established figure of 791. We will not have that until the end of the year.

On page 307 I find the following: "Publication of departmental reports and other material". Last year the estimate was $146,300. This year it is $156,300. Can the minister give us just exactly what these departmental reports consist of, because I see that the individual services have enormous amounts of money put aside for that purpose. The navy had $500,000 set aside for departmental reports. I have not actually checked the army and the air force, but I presume there are proportionately large sums set aside for those reports. Is there any particular

Supply-National Defence reason why this amount should be increased by $10,000, and what is the "other material" that is referred to?

The principal item in this vote for the publication of departmental reports is the expenditure for the bureau of current affairs. It issues a regular series of publications throughout the year which account for $140,000. Then there are the annual reports of the department in English and in French and the white paper, administrative amendments to directive documents and small matters of that kind. The major part of this, however, is for the publications of the bureau of current affairs.
To follow that up, what is the distribution of the publication of the bureau of current affairs? Is it distributed to all members of the armed services?

Some of the pamphlets that are published by the bureau of current affairs go to all members of the forces, some go to officers and some go to units as a group. Some of them are reserved by the queen's printer for sale to libraries, who make inquiries for them. The bulk however go to the troops.
Are any of these pamphlets monthly or bimonthly publications, or are they individual publications?
The standard practice is to put out two a month. In addition to that they publish a news report monthly.

I am not yet satisfied in regard to the matter I was speaking of a few minutes ago because on December 31, 1954, the white paper shows the number of these administrative personnel as 647. The number provided for in the estimates in 1954 was 769, or 122 more; but the number provided for in this year's estimates is 791, which is 144 more. I do not think the fact that a certain number of positions were not filled can be the real explanation of that.
When we get these figures, I like to think we can rely on them. This puts us in a difficulty. I do not know whether to take the figures from the blue book or from the white paper, or just what the situation is. It leaves a certain amount of ambiguity. It seems to me the department is estimating for many more people than it should be estimating for; otherwise the figure in the white paper is not correct.

I must apologize to the hon. member. I looked in the wrong column. The figure of 756 which I gave should have been 647, as the member stated. I understand there were a great number of vacancies, and fMr. Nesbitt.]

they are being filled gradually. As of May 31 this year the figure had arisen to 699; the rest are still unfilled.
Are any of these positions still not filled?

If we continue to find suitable people for these positions at the present rate they should all be filled by the end of this year. We have difficulty getting certain types of people for certain jobs, and they may remain vacant for quite a while.
How much of the amount of $2,529,601 which was voted last year was unspent?
The actual expenditure was $2,438,000.
That appears to be an obvious discrepancy. The difference between the two amounts is less than $100,000, but we are told that there were between 120 and 140 fewer people than appear on this list.

I think the discrepancy in last year's figures is explained by the fact that there was a general salary increase after the estimates had been prepared, and therefore it took more of the available money for fewer people.
There is a question I should like to ask the minister with regard to the details on page 308.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Has the committee any further discussion on departmental administration?
Would this be the proper place to discuss the historical section?
Is the hon. member referring to the army historical section or to any particular service?
It would refer more particularly to the army, but what I have to say would affect the other two services as well.
I think the hon. member might as well make his observations now.

In the first place I want to say that those responsible for the publications issued by the services deserved credit for what they have produced. The Canadian Army Journal for the army, the Roundel for the air force and the Crowsnest for the navy are all well-produced publications and I think serve a very effective purpose. However, I am more concerned with the material produced by the historical section which comes directly under the army.
A first-class piece of work has been done under the direction of Colonel Stacey in

providing a history of the services during the second world war. Beyond what Colonel Stacey and his assistants have produced in this connection they have contributed innumerable articles dealing with other aspects of Canadian history during other periods of time. The point I should like to take up with the minister may not at first make any great appeal to him, but I do present the case on this occasion for his consideration.
Along with the hon. member for Greenwood, about three years ago I interviewed the minister of national defence of that time and discussed the possibilities of producing a short history of the first world war. He agreed to discuss it with the historical section but nothing further was heard of the matter. I bring this matter to the attention of the present minister and ask him to give consideration to it. When I raised the question before it perhaps was not a suitable time, because the historical section was busily engaged in completing its work with regard to the second world war, but I understand that this has now reached completion.
They have a most competent staff and I suggest that before it is too late for the generation to which I belong some action might be taken to correct a grave deficiency that existed between the two wars, when steps were taken to produce a history of the first world war which did not get beyond one volume, after which apparently the project was dropped. Perhaps at this stage it is too late to talk about a detailed official history of the first world war running into several volumes, and that is not what I have in mind.
What I have in mind is something like the volume Colonel Stacey produced in 1948 entitled "The Canadian Army 1939-1945. Official Historical Summary." This volume relates the activities of the Canadian army during the course of the second world war to matters of general importance concerning Canada's war effort. The volume runs to about 350 pages and is an admirable publication serving the very purpose for which it was designed. I think that something along that line might very well be done with regard to the first world war. The historians might consider that it should be somewhat more elaborate, perhaps running to two volumes, but I would accept their advice in that regard.
The reason I raise the matter at this time is that the period of the first great war, from 1914 to 1918, represented for Canada its first such effort on a national scale. It was as a result of the effort of the Canadian people at that time that Canada achieved in the international field full recognition as a nation, though she had enjoyed this to a degree before. Had it not been for Canada's effort in
Supply-National Defence the first world war we would not have been represented at the council table when the peace treaties were signed, nor admitted as an independent nation to the league of nations. The argument for treating Canada as a separate nation was based upon her effort during the first world war. So without going into too great detail, I suggest that is one of the highlights in the history of the Canadian nation which is deserving of great attention.
I would say to those who think the first world war is over and forgotten that articles are appearing continually in the Canadian Army Journal, the Legionary and other magazines with reference to the first great war. Histories of Canada are being published at frequent intervals in which attention must of necessity be paid to the first great war. But for those who write with regard to that period there is no official Canadian history available.
In addition I would say to the minister that there are surviving in Canada several hundred thousand of those who served in the first world war. They look with envy upon the valuable books which were produced after the second world war concerning the navy, army and air force, and they express regret that the history of the period in which they were so active has not been written and presented to the Canadian people.
Consequently, for those and other reasons I might bring forth, I would ask the minister to give serious attention to this particular matter. I believe the historical section has the research material available. They have the trained staff ready and willing to embark on such an enterprise. I would hope that Colonel Stacey, if he is still actively engaged wtih the historical section, would be given the opportunity of directing the work, and the result would be a first-class contribution to Canadian history and Canadian military history.
We sometimes tend to play down military matters in Canada a little, as if we were not much interested in such matters and as if we were not a military nation. Yet when you read the history of this country you find that too frequently our destiny was determined by some military activity.
In that connection I would draw the attention of hon. members to the book published by Professor Stanley, of the Royal Military College at Kingston, on "Canada's Soldiers, 1604-1954", a period of 350 years, to which he gives the subtitle "The Military History of an Unmilitary People". In that history he brings forth for the first time a great deal of material which is not usually found in the histories of Canada, certainly the ones that have come to my attention. That volume is

Supply-National Defence a great contribution to Canadian military history, is well worth the study of those who are in the national defence department, and is of interest to the public generally.
We all are or should be aware of the value of a knowledge of the history of one's country. It so happens that part of that history at times has to concern itself with war. War is a destructive force in civilization and should not be played up from the standpoint of glorification or anything of that nature; but from the very fact that war involves sacrifice, and that as a result of the wars in which Canada has been engaged our country has gained in strength and our freedom has been maintained, there is no need for us ever to be ashamed of having histories of Canadian effort in wartime produced in this country.
I grant that there is as much interest in the history of other activities in a country; and as one who has always had an interest in history I get enjoyment from reading of other activities that Canadians have undertaken in building up this country over the centuries. Nevertheless there have been war activities, and the neglected portion in Canada's historical record has been the first great war. I hope now, before it becomes too late for this generation, the history of that war might be written.
It is fair to say that it will be written eventually, perhaps 20 or 50 years from now. People have an insatiable desire to know what has happened in the past. We read with interest nowadays stories about the Napoleonic wars and other wars that occurred in much more ancient times, and there continue to pour out from the printing presses histories of England, histories of the United States and histories of Canada. So, as I say, eventually the history of the Canadian effort in the first great war will be written. I simply propose to the minister that he give consideration to having it done in the near future, because he has a very able staff available to undertake this task.

Mr. Chairman, I should be very glad to take the hon. member's suggestion under consideration. As one who had some part in world war I, I have often received the same complaint he is making of not being able to find information about some phase of that war.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to come back to the matter I was discussing a few minutes ago. There seems to be a further discrepancy in the amount of $2,438,000 paid to 647 employees. The reason given as to why the amount spent was almost as much as the total amount provided for 

769 employees was that there had been a salary increase after the estimates had first been prepared. Has any increase in salaries taken place since the preparation of these estimates now before us listing the salaries referred to, particularly that of the deputy defence minister? Are those increases in salary not provided for or shown in the present list we have before us? Are they the present salaries?
Yes, they are.

If that is the case, why is it that $2,438,000 was paid out for 647 people in 1954-55, whereas $2,631,108 is the amount now projected to be paid out for 791 people? It is a difference of less than $200,000, but there is a big difference in the number of personnel.
Mr. Chairman, it is about six o'clock. Possibly the minister could get that statement during the dinner recess. After recess he might also be able to say something about another question which is worth looking into. The white paper shows the total of these civilian personnel at December 31, 1954, as 54,795. I should like to know how many of these civilian employees are shown in the estimates for 1954-55 and 1955-56. In other words, I should like to know what discrepancy there is between the numbers for whom we voted salaries in the estimates and the numbers shown as actually being on strength in 1954 in the white paper.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I understand that this is notice of the question.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. Chairman, immediately before the recess I had asked the minister a few questions regarding the civilian strength at headquarters and he was going to produce some figures in connection therewith.

In response to the hon. member's question, I cannot give definite figures but I am informed that, as far as departmental administration is concerned, the difference between the 791 personnel at a cost of $2,631,000 and the cost of the positions during the previous year is due to two factors. One is, as I have already stated, that actually a number of these positions are not filled or were not filled at the beginning of the year. Some of them will not be filled during the year.

The second factor is that these figures do not take into account the statutory increases which a great many of these people receive. The over-all figure of the cost of these positions is arrived at without regard to the statutory increases of the various employees, which amount to quite a large sum if the increases are granted and if the positions are occupied. That is the imponderable. Some of the positions are occupied and some are not.

It seems to me what that comes down to is that we are being asked to vote $2,631,000 for a group of positions outlined here, and at the salaries outlined, and we should be able to take it that the amounts are absolutely definite. But then the minister tells us that some of these positions are not filled and as a result they think the sum of $2,631,000 will be close to the amount they are going to expend. Surely we can get something more definite than that.

Perhaps I might say, as I have already mentioned, that there are a number of imponderables in these computations. The estimators who made up the estimates for 1954-55 estimated a sum of $2,529,000 on the same basis as the $2,631,000 was estimated this year, making some allowance for positions that probably could not be filled, statutory increases, and so on, and we actually spent $2,400,000 odd. Therefore the over-all picture is pretty closely parallel.
It is very difficult to give specific figures for items such as statutory increases when we do not know how many of a given classification are entitled to them, and when we do not know how many vacant positions there may be in a given classification at any particular time. While we have vacant positions when we start the year, there are also vacant positions which arise during the year and they are not filled right away. It is pretty difficult to lay it down right on the line, but I should think the amount spent in the previous year in relation to the estimate for that year would indicate that by and large we are fairly close to the mark, and it is on the same basis that the amount of $2,631,000 is estimated.

I would say just the reverse of what the minister said. As a matter of fact they laid down definite salaries for 769 persons and they only had 647. That is 122 less, but they spent within less than $100,000 of the amount estimated. When I asked for an explanation of why 647 people got as much money as we had voted for 769, the minister said that to begin with quite a number of the positions had not been filled. Then he came along with another explanation
Supply-National Defence that there had been increases in salaries in the meantime. But then I pointed out that for the present 791 positions the vote is only $2,631,000, less than $200,000 more. Subtracting 647 from 791, there are 144 more people at increased salaries.
Therefore the explanation just does not add up arithmetically. There is something wrong with it. If the list of amounts shown here is completely wrong, then I would say we are being asked to vote money under false pretences. The list includes a deputy minister at $20,000, two associate deputy ministers at $12,000, and so on. Is the minister trying to tell me these are not the present salaries of these people, and the same thing right down the line? I do not think he will try to say that. I would say the explanation he has just given really does not hold water, and that from what we have been told so far you cannot reconcile the amount of $2,438,
000	paid last year for 647 people with a vote of $2,631,000 for 791 people. Arithmetically it does not add up, and we have had no answer so far to show what the correct situation is. I would not be surprised if there was a perfectly logical explanation, but we have not heard it so far.

I have given a number of factors which, put together, I think make a very reasonable explanation. The hon. member referred to the deputy minister's salary. This is one of the 791 positions. The deputy minister is getting a salary of $20,000 a year. He will be retiring on the 1st of July. Another deputy minister at a lesser salary will be coming in on the 15th of August. These are imponderable things that you cannot reduce to dollars and cents. After all, you have nearly 800 positions and a great many of them change. In addition, these are only estimates; these are not the sums that will necessarily be paid.
All I am saying is that for the reasons
1	gave before dinner and the one I added since dinner, the fact is, as the estimates indicate, that 1954-55 was fairly close to the mark. I do not think it is possible, and I do not think any good purpose would be served by continuing to try to reconcile specifically each of these 791 salaries, with all the imponderables of the positions filled, the positions vacant, the positions which cannot be filled, the statutory increases and so on, and try to reduce it to dollars and cents. If the hon. member can do that he is better than I am. I can only leave it in that position.

I am not in a position where I need to do it, but I think the minister is in a position where he needs to do it.

Supply-National Defence
I am in a position where I need to be sure that I am paying a man what he has earned and what he is entitled to get.

When we have certain figures presented to us in the committee and we are voting money to pay these people, we should be in a position to know that there are 791 people and that their total salaries amount to so much. We should vote that amount. However, now we discover that is not the situation. Some of these people are not there at all, and some of them may not be receiving these salaries at all. As I said, I believe in effect we are being asked to vote money under what really amounts to false pretences.

The hon. gentleman should know how this operates. The civil service commission approves the establishment and approves the scales of salaries. The statutes provide that if the chief of an employee who has been engaged under civil service regulations, and who has given satisfaction during the statutory period, certifies that he is entitled to an increase of $5, $10 or $15 per month, then that increase is granted. However, it is conditional upon there being a certificate submitted to the treasury board from the chief that the man has given satisfactory service. I happen to know that, because I have to sign these certificates for the employees in the privy council office. They are brought to me by the immediate chief of the person concerned, and it is only when I have signed a certificate which goes to the treasury board that the increase is authorized.
Now, if we were voting money to pay for past services it would have to be absolutely precise. But as the minister has said, he is asking parliament to appropriate money that will be sufficient to pay these salaries under conditions as they may develop. It may be that there are, and it usually is the case that there are, some of these amounts that are not expended. It happens that there are some who do not get the certificates which, if they got them, would entitle them to the increase in salary.
Then these certificates are not issued at any one period during the year. They come at the anniversary of the entry into the service of the civil servant concerned. It may be that he will have for a part of the fiscal year a salary of so many dollars per month, and for the last three, four, five or six or eight months of the fiscal year a larger salary than he had in the previous months. Those are what the minister has referred to as the imponderables.


The deputy minister who will replace the retiring deputy minister will commence at the initial salary fixed under the establishment that has been set up and will, from anniversary to anniversary of his entry into the service, if his minister recommends it, get the approved statutory increases. The maximum for the position is $20,000 and the initial salary is, I believe, $17,500. I have no doubt, from my personal knowledge of the capacity and devotion to duty of the gentleman who has been appointed to the position of deputy minister, that at each anniversary of his entry into the service, his minister will certify that his services have been of a character to warrant the so-called statutory increases.
The treasury board has been called the watchdog, and it is the watchdog. It requires written certificates with respect to the application of these provisions that apply to the statutory increases in salary.

The Prime Minister was not here during the whole of the discussion, and therefore is not apprised of the sort of basic discrepancy about which I have been complaining. The imponderables about which he has spoken would amount to possibly a few thousand dollars, and I quite understand that. But there is a basic discrepancy which the imponderables, changes in salary and so forth, would not explain in any case so far as this particular vote is concerned. It is for that reason I have been pressing this thing for some considerable time. It seems to me that these votes which are presented to us should be as close, both so far as the individual items which make them up are concerned and so far as the total amounts are concerned, as it is possible to get them. Last year we voted for 769 positions at definite salaries, and then we find from the white paper that actually there were only 647 people.
There were 714 as of December 31.
As of December 31, the white paper shows 647.
That is at headquarters, but not for the whole category. They are in other places besides headquarters.

That is the vote we are talking about. Up to this minute the minister never disputed the figure of 647; that is the figure we have been talking about, and he has never raised any question about it. Perhaps that is the explanation. As I said before,
I was sure there must be some other explanation than the one that had been given, and perhaps that is it. There are some people who

appear on pages 306 and 307 of the blue book who do not appear in the list of 647 at page 30 of the white paper. That may be the logical explanation, but certainly we have not had any explanation up to date. It would appear this is a quite serious discrepancy in the amount of money paid and in the number of people employed.
Carried.
No, Mr. Chairman. Is the minister going to say there are more than 647 people covered?

I said that as of December 31, 1954, there were 714, including all those people in this particular category. The figure the hon. member has been quoting is for headquarters, and the administrative offices are not all at headquarters.

I think perhaps we have finally obtained an explanation of what looks like a quite serious discrepancy. In addition to the 647 shown on page 30 of the white paper there are enough more in other parts of the service to make up 714, and whose jobs appear under departmental administration at pages 306 and 307?
The figure is at the bottom of page 29 of the white paper.

At the bottom of page 29 is shown the total number of people, 714, in administration other than inspection services. If the minister is stating that is the total number of people covered here, and the number who have been paid, then that may be a reasonable explanation. But it has taken a long time to get that far. Then the white paper at page 29 shows 54,795 civilian employees. How many civilian employees are shown in the estimates for the years 195455 and 1955-56?

The positions for which salaries were detailed in the estimates for 1954-55 numbered 47,678, and for the present year 51,608. Those are positions detailed in the estimates. The figure of 54,795 as of December 31, 1954, at page 29 of the white paper, is made up of (a) casuals, not detailed in the estimates and (b) staff of the defence research board, likewise not detailed in the estimates. These are not handled in the estimates in the same way as the rest of the staff.
I should like to mention a local problem in my own riding having to do with a road.

I think the hon. member is out of order, because we will have an item under which that could be discussed. I know
Supply-National Defence the matter the hon. member is referring to.
I would have no objection to discussing it now, but it deals with a road to a radio station and is connected with the air force.
Very well; we shall discuss it later.

I notice at page 306 of the estimates an amount for a director of public relations. Are there any civilian employees under the director of public relations, or are they all service personnel? If they are, then how many service personnel in each of the services come under the jurisdiction of the director?

Each service has its own director of public relations in that service, and his staff are members of the service. The director of public relations is a civilian who correlates and co-ordinates the work of the other public relations officers.
Does the head of public relations in each service come under the chief of staff or under the director of public relations?
Each public relations officer in each service is under his own chief of staff. However, they also work in close co-operation and co-ordination with the director of public relations.
Is it the chief of staff or the director of public relations who has final authority over public relations staff?

Technically speaking I would say that each public relations officer is under his own chief of staff. Some of the publicity comes to me, and it always comes through the co-ordinator. They all work together. They work with him and he works with them. But technically speaking I would say that each public relations officer is under his own service.
How long has the office of director of public relations been in existence?
It was instituted during the war and has been almost continuous ever since. Offhand I could not give the date.

Perhaps I might ask my other questions when we reach the various services. I would still like to know the number of personnel in each of the services, but I will be content to ask those questions later, if desired.

Information at the bottom of page 307 would indicate that there has been a gradual increase in the number of stenographers, typists and clerks. I know that in certain cases reclassification takes place so that the increase shown may not be as great as would appear at first

Supply-National Defence glance. But at pages 307, 309, 313, 325, 337 and 338 we note a considerable increase in this kind of help in the department. It would seem that the combination of typists, stenographers, clerks and publications would indicate a continuation of the paper war. I note that the amount spent for publications in 1951-52 was $71,000; 1952-53, $103,000; 1953-54,	$126,000;	1954-55,	$146,300 and
1955-56, $156,300.
In each year over the past four or five years there has been a steady increase in this type of expenditure. What steps are taken within the department, or what control is exercised by the senior officials in the department, in connection with the type of appointment which is reflected by this increase in numbers and by the increase in expenditures on this type of publication, and so forth?

I think I outlined fairly clearly in my remarks yesterday the procedure for establishing a new position. First of all there is the committee in the department which screens the prospective position, studies it and makes such recommendations as it sees fit. When that has been done, the report, if favourable, goes to the civil service commission, and they do their own studying and screening of the request for the position and make their report. When that has been made, if the report is favourable, then the question of the position goes to treasury board, and they are the final authority who authorize or do not authorize its establishment.
Therefore it can be taken that positions are not lightly created and, in fact, are not approved unless there is genuine need for them. The department has grown; I think the figures will indicate that the growth in the numbers by categories is not out of line with the growth in civilian personnel in these offices.

Will the minister indicate where the actual request for appointments on this level is initiated? Does it come from the upper brackets of the officers of the department? Where is the actual request initiated?

The initiation of a new
position in a branch comes to the head of the branch from the particular person who seeks to have the position established. The head of the branch then considers it, and if he thinks it has merit he sends it to the assistant deputy minister in charge of personnel, who then looks into it, and if he approves then it goes to the committee I have mentioned.
Has the minister ever considered the appointment of a board within his own department to review what appears to be continuing applications of this type for increases in personnel?

There are a number of these committees. In fact there is one in each service. They are all competent committees and they sit from time to time. In addition to reviewing the applications of which I have been speaking, they also review existing positions to see if they are still needed and if they are being utilized. Therefore we keep as close a check in the department on the growth of the staff as can reasonably be expected.

Has that work been extended at all into an investigation into departmental procedures from the paper standpoint? I have illustrated a continuing increase in expenditure of one type. Is there any over-all committee which is conducting any check on this type of expenditure?

There is no over-all committee which covers the whole field, as the hon. member has suggested, but committees are set up from time to time to make specific studies where it looks as though they should be made. For example, we had one not long ago studying publications. But there is not an actual over-all committee that surveys the whole department in one operation.
I would suggest to the minister that if this type of expenditure continues to increase in this way we might consider appointing a committee to look into the work of that other committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee through with departmental administration?

I should like to ask a question supplementary to the one asked by my colleague. The question of outside investigation by efficiency companies has been raised before, and the predecessor of the present minister pooh-poohed it and would have no part of it. I am interested to learn, from what the minister has just said, that there apparently is no over-all committee surveying the question of employment, the allocation of duties, and so on, notwithstanding that, if my memory serves me there are over 30,000 civilian employees in the department. I understand there are merely these ad hoc committees surveying various problems from time to time. That is my understanding of what the minister said. That seems to me to leave the possibility of gaps, and to fail to grapple in a comprehensive way with what appears to be a huge problem of organization.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we pass to inspection services?
I wish the minister would comment on that.

I think I have said all that I can say. There are complement committees -a number of them-which together cover the whole field. There are other matters in the department that ad hoc committees deal with from time to time, such as publications. But on the personnel side the complement committees, who sit all the time and who are specialists, taken together-one committee could not do it all-cover the whole field.

The minister speaks about the committees being specialists. Will he explain how they become specialists in this kind of organization? In the first place, are they service officers whose primary duties would presumably be in organization on the military side?
