I understand that they are composed of service personnel and civilian personnel who have been trained in personnel work. Some of them are graduates of the Harvard school of business. They are all well trained in the type of work in which they are engaged.

But the co-ordination
apparently is more or less accidental, or at any rate there is no body which co-ordinates the various ad hoc committees which are dealing with special problems.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we pass to inspection services?
May I have an answer to that question?
I understand the co-ordination work is done by an officer on the deputy minister's staff who is known as the superintendent of establishments.

One other question in connection with this particular aspect of the estimates; has any survey been conducted throughout the whole department as to the use of various new mechanical means of handling the massive paper work that must be handled by the department? We read daily of large corporations which make considerable savings in personnel and expenses by utilization of mechanical devices in office work. Has the department looked into questions of that kind?

There is a man under the assistant deputy minister, administration, who is a specialist in the field to which the hon. member has referred, and who spends his time in an effort to shorten procedures
Supply-National Defence and save paper work and do the various things that the hon. member has suggested.

Does the
minister feel that from the office standpoint his department is up to date in connection with the new types of equipment that are available?
I would say reasonably so, yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On inspection services.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two questions I should like to ask under this heading. I will outline what I have in mind and then perhaps the minister can give an answer. Set out on page 308 are four categories of inspectors. There are inspectors, grade 1; inspecting officers, grade 3; inspecting officers, grade 2; and inspecting officers, grade 1. There are between 40 and 50 of these. Then a little further down the page we find inspectors of stores, grade 4, of which there are 79; inspectors of stores, grade 3, of which there are 327; inspectors of stores, grade 2, of which there are 466; and inspectors of stores, grade 1, of which there are 117, making a grand total for inspectors of stores of 989. Then when we refer to the various services specifically we find that the air force has 25 inspectors of stores and the navy 16. These are of varying gradations, grades 1, 2 and 3.
In all the defence estimates there seems to be a total of 1,069 inspectors of stores, which is a formidable total. I was wondering if the minister could give us an outline of what these inspectors do and where their duties are carried out; how long they work, exactly what is their work, and so on.

The members of the inspection service of our department include highly-trained engineers, chemists and technicians who are located at various points across Canada. The services maintain six chemical laboratories, a very complete electronics laboratory, a physical testing laboratory, two gauge laboratories, three proof ranges, a tire testing laboratory and many other incidentals. The direct value of the stores still to be inspected as of March 31 of this year was $518 million, with the number of contracts being 5,111.
These men are placed in their positions on qualifications established by the civil service commission, which account for the different grades. The different grades depend on the type of work in which the men are engaged. This work represents a major effort of our department, as naturally we have to have everything inspected before we accept and pay for it, and a good deal of the inspection

Supply-National Defence has to be done in laboratories, much of it while the commodity is being produced.

If the minister has not the information now possibly he can give it the next time his estimates are being considered, but I should like to have a sort of break-down of what these people do. The word "inspector" is a vague sort of word and would seem to suggest someone who was inspecting stores periodically. I take it from the minister's remarks that this category would include people who test materials received by the various services, materials being used in building contracts and so on. The personnel set out on page 308 under inspection services represents a cost of nearly $3-5 million, which is a tidy sum indeed for inspection purposes.
I should like to know how many of these inspectors actually go around checking stores on hand in the various establishments, how many are actually testing materials, and so on. I think that information would be most helpful.

I cannot at the moment give the details the hon. member has requested, but perhaps I can give him some idea of what is involved.
This service is charged with the responsibility of ensuring that materials and equipment ordered by the armed services are furnished in accordance with the specifications, *or suggesting changes in specifications to bring them in line with manufacturing practices, for investigating facilities of firms to produce specific requirements, for interpreting to the contractor government specifications and the technical requirements of the contract, for recommending for or against design changes requested by manufacturers and to recommend cancellation of a contract when it is determined that the manufacturer is not meeting his commitments. In addition to the above, reciprocal inspection is carried out on behalf of the United States armed services and in connection with the NATO and Colombo plans.
That is a general statement of the work they do.

Possibly the next time the committee meets the minister will be able to give us a further break-down, because there seems to be an extraordinarily large number of persons involved in this particular branch of the defence department. I for one would like to have further explanation at a later date.

There is an item on page 310 covering payments for municipal and public utility services, and
similar items will be found on pages 319, 329, 333, 334 and 340. I assume that this covers water services, probably sewer services and so on furnished by municipalities in which defence department buildings are located. Are these payments based upon the tariffs of the municipalities, or are they a type of grant to the municipality? Is it in any way tied in with the grants made to municipalities in lieu of taxes as provided by the Municipal Grants Act?

This vote represents sums paid to municipalities for water and services of various kinds. Such sums are taken into consideration when grants are being made under the Municipal Grants Act. There is an adjustment made so we are not paying twice for the same thing, or for something we do not get. In certain circumstances we make contracts for the services from the municipalities as any customer would.

In other words you are paying for the services based on the tariff of the municipality. Is a capital contribution ever made toward the establishment of these services, in the same way that an owner of real estate must make capital payment for the establishment of services?

Yes, we have in some cases, under certain circumstances where it seemed to be in our best interests. It is the only thing to do in certain cases, depending on the situation. We have made capital contributions for the services that we use jointly with the municipality, such as a water plant, or a sewerage or disposal plant.
I understand there are cases where simply the cost of the service is paid and no capital contribution is made.
That is correct.

I should like to ask the minister a question or two about irregularities and losses that have occurred in No. 11 works company, R.C.E. I assume it would be appropriate to pursue those inquiries under "Inspection services", or would it be more appropriate to do so under the army item?
If the hon. member does not mind, I would rather deal with that under the army.
Are these inspectors we have been discussing living in camp or do they have to supply their own domicile on these salaries? Some of the salaries are rather low.

For the most part the inspectors, except those who work in the laboratories testing materials, as I have mentioned, are appointed to ensure quality. They do not live in military camps. Most of them live in proximity to plants where they are stationed, where there are contracts for defence services. They are sent to plants from which we would buy production.
Two hundred dollars a month does not seem to be a very large salary for an inspector who has to find his own living quarters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On Royal Canadian Navy- active force and general.

A year ago concern was expressed regarding the supply of officers for the Royal Canadian Navy. In order to meet what was then a seeming shortage, a new scheme known as the "Venture plan" was introduced. I had the opportunity of visiting that Venture college, and it is an extremely well run college with an excellent type of young men coming into the service from all parts of Canada. But I am still rather concerned regarding the supply of officers for the Royal Canadian Navy.
I notice in a return which was included on page 27 of last year's white paper that the number of men in training in the various schools for officers in the Royal Canadian Navy amounted to 1,287. That did not include the Venture scheme. When I look at the similar return on page 26 of this year's white paper I notice that there are 1,241, a decrease of 46, in spite of the fact that Venture college has been established and I believe there are in the neighbourhood of 100 young men taking that training. So it looks to me as though the situation has not been met yet, and that the sources of supply of officers for the Royal Canadian Navy are not improving.
I am also concerned regarding a return which was tabled in the house on March 7 showing the graduates of the various service colleges. Over the past six years the young men entering those colleges have averaged 220 a year. But out of that number, in the last two years-and I am dealing only with the last two years because the colleges have not been operating much longer than that and would not be turning out graduates-in 1952-53 only 11 of these 220 went into the Royal Canadian Navy and last year, 1953-54, there were only 12 commissioned into the Royal Canadian Navy.
It does not seem to me that the navy is getting anything like its fair proportion of the young men entering the service colleges. If from all sources there is a reduction in the
Supply-National Defence number of those under training this year, in spite of the fact that Venture college has been started, has the situation deteriorated or do these figures not really represent the supply? We are getting only 11 from the naval college. Eleven or twelve per year certainly will not take care of the wastage. I wonder if the minister could say how many young officers were commissioned into the navy last year, that is out of this total of 1,287 who were in training in the various intakes.
I am sorry that I have not the figures set up in that way, but I shall be glad to get them.

Could the minister inform
the committee as to the situation? I am not so concerned regarding the numbers, but I have given the numbers to illustrate the reason for my concern. It seems that the situation is deteriorating. If that is not so, perhaps the minister would inform us.

The figures the hon. member quoted are not quite complete, owing to the fact that the executive officers after the second year go directly into the navy, whereas engineers for example continue on. I have not the figures here, but I am told the situation is rather tight.

I realize that executive officers go out in the second year, and I have included those in the two years. From the service colleges seven went who passed last year, and five from the four-year group. Of course that is only a trickle, and there must be a much greater demand.

Each year for several years -at least six or seven-I expressed considerable concern at the proportion of service personnel in each of the services engaged in administrative and other jobs of that sort, as compared with the number of people in actual fighting units. Ordinarily we have had a fair amount of discussion about that. Perhaps as a means of meeting that criticism, in last year's white paper a breakdown was given on page 23 for each of the services, showing how the service personnel were employed. As far as the navy is concerned it was as follows:
Navy
Units for NATO, Korean force and defence
of coastal waters	 5,900
Training staffs and trainees	 6,200
Commands and administration	 1,500
Dockyards and bases	 3,300
16,900
I note that in this year's white paper the breakdown of the employment of navy, army and air force personnel has been omitted.
4968	HOUSE OF
Supply*-National Defence 1 wonder whether the minister could give us comparable figures for the same date this year as last. That would be December 31, 1954, instead of December 31, 1953; or if he has figures for a later date that would be even better.
I shall have to get the breakdown set up the way it was last year.

When the minister is getting that information will he also get it for the army and air force, because I shall be asking the same question in connection with those services. I should like to observe at this time that I think it was a mistake that the breakdown was dropped from this year's white paper. I do not understand why, once the giving of such figures had become established, they were omitted, because it just takes more time to get the figures during the period we are discussing the estimates.

I have three questions I should like to put to the minister with respect to the naval service. The first is a general one. Looking through the estimates, it is rather surprising to me to see the vast number of civilian personnel used by the navy. Going back to the days when I was an active member of that service, it would seem to me that a great many of these positions now apparently filled by civilian personnel were filled by service personnel. I suppose the question naturally arises, what difference does it make? As I see the matter, it makes this difference. For example, let us take some of the figures on page 317. At the very top there is an estimate for 11 pipe fitters, the same number as there were last year. The difference in the estimated cost between last year and this year is the difference between $28,465 last year and $42,463 this year.
I presume this is due to the increased cost of hiring civilian personnel, which does not arise if the personnel are in uniform. You will find the same thing all the way down the page, in practically every item. Take refrigeration mechanics. There are two in the estimates for this year and last year. Last year the cost was $7,894 and this year it is $8,808. The next item is one repair maintenance man at a cost last year of $2,631 and this year $3,318. Further down we have stewards and steward cooks. One would normally expect to find the people doing these jobs in uniform. Last year there were four stewards at a cost of $8,748. This year there are the same number and the cost is $9,672.
On page 316 we find that there are a great number of messmen, an increase from 130 to 164. Then there are such items as 

"painters, brush hand", "painters, finish", "painters' helpers", and a great many others. One could go on for 15 or 20 minutes, but I do not intend to take the time of the house to do that. However, I point out that many of these jobs, as 1 recall them, were formerly carried out by service personnel and I see no reason why they cannot be carried out by enlisted personnel. The main advantage would be saving the increases in wages which I am sure, if you add them all, amount to a tremendously large sum of money. That is the first question on which I should like some comment.
The second has to do with a particularly interesting item I find at the bottom of page 314. I see that this year we have an increase from 267 to 270 in the number of civilian chauffeurs for the navy. On the face of it one would wonder what on earth the navy could do with 270 chauffeurs. I have no doubt it may be a somewhat ambiguous term and covers certain other duties that one would not normally expect of a chauffeur. However, I am sure the minister will give us the explanation. The item below is "chauffeurs, motor truck drivers", and there is an increase this year from 26 to 51. I can quite understand why the navy would require motor truck drivers, but I am a little curious as to why the number should be just about double. As far as chauffeurs are concerned, we have 270 this year and there were 267 last year. On page 313 we find there are four chauffeurs in the United Kingdom. I should like to hear an explanation of what the Royal Canadian Navy is doing with four civilian chauffeurs in England.
My third question is one I previously put to the minister. How many naval personnel are engaged in public relations?

I would not want the minister to think the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for Oxford are the only members interested in how the navy spends its money. When the minister is answering some of the questions that have been asked, will he tell the committee why the navy spends $3,340 a year on a man for holding on. The item will be found on page 315, being the sixth from the bottom.
I wonder whether the hon. member would let me deal with these other questions first.
He receives $3,340, which is an increase over last year.

I understand that the navy does not have naval drivers for cars; they use civilians. Therefore the drivers, in this case called chauffeurs, are simply the drivers

of the various vehicles that are utilized by the navy or else they are motor truck chauffeurs for navy trucks. With regard to the other question as to civilian artificers and tradesmen, to whom the hon. member referred first, and as to why they are not in uniform, I understand when men whose skills are required on shore, and there is no necessity for them to have sea duty or fleet experience, civilians are engaged.

I suggested that many of these personnel should be in the navy because of the great increase in cost this year over last year involved in employing civilians. As we all know, the cost of civilian labour is increasing from year to year. If a lot of these people were in the service that extra cost would not necessarily be involved. Then, too, if they were in the service they would also have the advantage of a retirement pension in due course, plus certain other advantages that service personnel enjoy.
That is particularly noticeable in the case of the chauffeurs. This year there are 270 and last year there were only three fewer. Last year the estimate was $621,000 and this year, with only three chauffeurs more, the estimate is $717,000, almost $100,000 more. If naval personnel were used as drivers there would be a saving of very close to $100,000 right there. I would be interested to hear the minister's comment on that and also on the size of the naval establishment in the United Kingdom that requires four chauffeurs.

I cannot answer the last question, because I do not know how their classifications run in regard to civilians employed as against uniformed personnel. The fact is I am informed that notwithstanding the increases in these civilian posts in the last few years, the difference between the pay of civilian employees and uniformed service personnel is still quite great. I mentioned yesterday that the reason we use civilian employees in so many positions is because there is a wide difference between the cost of maintaining a serviceman and the cost of a civilian in this type of employment. I think ordinarily a civilian earns around $2,600. These 270 chauffeurs costing $717,206 work at about $2,600 each, and a serviceman of the same type or class to do the same work costs about $3,600 per year.
In so far as these chauffeurs are concerned I see below this item mention of motor truck drivers-what sort of vehicles do they operate? Are they staff cars or what?

Well, they have an assortment of vehicles. The chauffeurs operate all the types of vehicles used around a dockyard, and by the navy. There are passenger
Supply-National Defence cars, station wagons, buses, jeeps, trucks, ambulances and various other types of vehicles.

The minister has said, I think, that they have certain comparable figures in relation to civilian and uniformed personnel. He pointed out that something had just been worked out with respect to the cost of the serviceman as a chauffeur versus a civilian. Has there been an actual, careful survey made throughout all these classifications to see whether it is really cheaper to hire a civilian, despite the greatly increased cost of labour, or to bring a man into the service? If so, has that survey been made recently? There does seem to be a great difference in the cost between the estimates of this year and the estimates of last year.
This matter of chauffeurs may seem rather trivial. Perhaps the hon. member for Greenwood would correct me if I am mistaken, but I understand that many a mickle make a muckle. It seems to me that surely the department could dispense with a great number of these chauffeurs. I understand that senior officers, for prestige purposes, have to have chauffeurs, but it would seem to me that many of the more junior officers might very well drive their own cars. It is a small item, but the number does seem rather large.

I understand that the
vehicles which are utilized by all branches of the navy, and by other services, and types of drivers are matters that are considered by a committee. This committee says whether or not they are justified.
In connection with the other point raised by the hon. member, I think it has been found more economical to have one man assigned to drive a car than to have different people driving service cars intermittently. These men are engaged full time. Under the pool arrangement a man is responsible for his car or truck, or whatever vehicle he has been entrusted with, and is closely checked.
Probably the minister overlooked the other question I had asked. What is the number of personnel engaged in public relations in the navy?

Perhaps while I am giving the figures for the navy I could give the figures for the other services, since I have them here now. In the navy the total number is 13 service personnel and 9 civilians, a total of 22; in the army, 55 service personnel and 9 civilians, a total of 64; in the Royal Canadian Air Force-this includes those in Europe-45 service personnel and 7 civilians, a total of 52.

Supply-National Defence

I thank the minister for that information. In so far as public relations men are concerned, could the minister give a brief outline of their duties? Are they required to write certain releases for the press or are they required to go out and speak at public gatherings? What type of work are they generally given?

The duties of a public relations director are to maintain a flow of ordinary news items of interest from his particular service to the public; meet representatives of the press, radio, and television; prepare reports on training and on new equipment; issue press releases and from time to time feature stories of their service; to oversee publicity photography for the service; to prepare radio tapes for use in making the service known, and the usual contact work in the establishment of press relations.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on behalf of one particular group of civilians who work for the Royal Canadian Navy. I refer to the prevailing rates employees at the ammunition depot at Renous, New Brunswick. The matter I have in mind is one which is well covered in a letter dated June 13, 1955, copies of which were sent to ten or a dozen members of this house including the Minister of National Defence. I would ask him to look at that letter of June 13, which was sent by the Renous federal union No. 239, to see if something cannot be done to meet the complaint of these employees. In my experience here, Mr. Chairman, it is a frequent grievance of prevailing rate employees, and it is one about which complaint apparently has to be made. I know one of the answers I may get-and the minister may get the same answer from his advisers, because I have had it before-is that this is a matter in which any other department takes guidance or advice from the Department of Labour. We are told that they ask the Department of Labour to go into the area and find out the prevailing rates for people doing the same or a similar kind of work. But it seems that the comparisons are made with the poorer paid rather than the medium or better paid workers doing what the workers feel is a comparable kind of work.
I shall not take time to go into the various details involving hours of work, superannuation benefits and other points which are covered in the letter to which I have referred.
It does seem to me, however, that the Minister of National Defence has some responsibility to deal with the matter. I hope he will give me the assurance that he will look at 

the letter and see if this complaint cannot be met without further delay.
He will recall that on a previous occasion the hon. member for Cape Breton South raised this matter. On his behalf and my own, as well as on behalf of these employees, I am asking the minister to take another look at it.

In principle, the hon.
member answered his own question when he said that in the matter of prevailing rates we rely on the Department of Labour. I am aware of the letter to which the hon. member refers, and I shall be glad to do what I have been doing upon occasion, namely, discuss the situation with the Minister of Labour. I do not try just to pass all responsibility to that department, but we must be sure to keep some sort of rate basis that will be appropriate to the particular part of the country. But we do not take the primary responsibility for the fixing of those rates. In this particular case I have read the letter and I shall discuss the matter with the Minister of Labour.

Mr. Chairman, I
would like to change the subject by referring to page 319, where it deals with the acquisition and construction of buildings and works. Perhaps in the interests of brevity we might consider at the same time army buildings.
A problem is gradually developing in cities and towns across Canada in connection with property on which are located buildings used by the Department of National Defence. Many of these buildings were constructed many years ago as barracks and armouries, at a time when property was comparatively low in value. Those buildings are now located in the midst of cities and towns, with a resultant loss of revenue to the municipalities concerned. They do not serve any particular purpose, so far as the forces are concerned.
As an example let me refer to my own constituency of London, which the minister visited recently and with which he is familiar. We have in London a naval depot known as H.M.C.S. Prevost located on perhaps the most valuable downtown piece of property in the city. We have also an armouries located on equally valuable property, and we have an area headquarters for the army.
What is the policy of the department with respect to these properties when the buildings erected thereon outlive their usefulness? The minister is no doubt familiar with the area headquarters building. It is antiquated, as is the naval headquarters. We have in London Wolseley barracks, which has ample property on which to consolidate at least the army part of the set-up. Surely other

property equally suitable but less valuable could be found for the naval headquarters.
I am asking the minister to comment generally as to the policy of the department concerning the removal of such buildings from valuable downtown property as and when they become outmoded. What are the department's plans for the area headquarters in London, and for the building now occupied by the naval division?

As most hon. members realize, the question of administration accommodation is constantly before us. It is never fully resolved because its priority in the matter of the allocation of money is of a relatively low order. We are trying to improve conditions in various places as fast as we can, but we are very much in arrears due to the fact that very little was done during the war; and because of our high expenditures for defence purposes at the present time. At the present time we are endeavouring to obtain a site for H.M.C.S. Prevost and I can only say I hope we will succeed.
In regard to the other matter the hon. member mentioned, let me say that I cannot make any promise because there are many similar situations. The only thing I can say is that we are trying to remedy the most urgent cases first.

Is the minister's answer a statement that the policy of the department is, wherever possible and as money is available, to release valuable downtown property for commercial purposes rather than to occupy it for military purposes.

If we do not need the property we certainly will not endeavour to hold it. But that raises the whole question of downtown properties, particularly armouries. Most of the major facilities in our cities are downtown, and these properties have become valuable. Many of the buildings are still in good condition, and we would suffer a heavy loss if we were to undertake to replace at today's costs those buildings which do not require replacement. However, if it is property we do not really need we try always to co-operate with the municipalities.
As I have pointed out, the governing factor is money. Downtown property is high in price, but so is the cost of new buildings to supplant downtown buildings. It is just a case of adjusting the money we have available to those places which need it most.

May I ask
a further question in that connection. I shall mention a situation which falls within the four corners of the minister's statement, but
Supply-National Defence concerning which we have had no action for a considerable length of time. I refer specifically to the Long Branch rifle ranges in the county of Peel. I am convinced that the price that could be obtained for the property by the department would replace, in a slightly more distant location, all the facilities the department now enjoys.
Undoubtedly the procrastination of the department in answering the request of the municipality in that area is proving a very great hardship. That property now is certainly among the most valuable lakeshore properties left in the district of metropolitan Toronto. I would seriously suggest to the minister that if the policy he has laid down is the one to be pursued by the department, then the Long Branch situation can be fitted squarely into the four corners of the policy and some relief might be granted to that particular area in the very near future.

I think I can assure the hon. member that there has been no procrastination since I have been minister, because I started to look into this situation as soon as I became minister. The facts of the situation are that while it is a very valuable property, it is also the only rifle range we have in that whole area. As Minister of National Defence I have had to take the view that, until we can find a suitable area for a rifle range, I cannot very well give up the present site.
I have not stopped there but have had a study made-I must say unsuccessfully-of other alternatives that might be available close to Toronto. We are now engaged in preparing the necessary facilities and ranges at Camp Borden. When they are completed we shall not be requiring the Long Branch area, and I presume that under the usual crown procedures it will be disposed of. From the last report I have received, which was some weeks ago, that will not be until possibly next spring or summer.

Does that mean the minister may be in a position to commit the department to a date not later than the summer of 1956 for disposal of the Long Branch range It seems to me that would be adequate time. After all, Camp Borden has been in existence and used for that particular purpose we are talking about since early in the first world war. In addition, there will be no sacrifices required by the members of the militia units. The changes in methods of travel since the building of the Long Branch rifle range I am sure place Camp Borden almost within as easy reach of the centre of Toronto as Long Branch was at the time of the construction of the range there. As a matter of fact, with the construction of
4972	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence highway No. 400, even keeping within the speed limit I would estimate that Camp Borden is only 1J to 13 hours away. Therefore I hope the minister can make a definite commitment as to when that land will be available to the municipality.

I do not want to be put in the position of making a definite commitment. I have seen too much of construction since I came into this particular office to make promises or fix specific dates. All I was endeavouring to do was state with frankness what I am trying to do. If everything comes to pass which I have mentioned I would hope that by next summer or fall we shall be in a position to take up new quarters, and I would not want to go beyond that. I think my hon. friend will have to rest his case there.
I have the figures for the breakdown of the services by categories for the hon. member for Calgary North. These show the employment of the active forces on December 31 last. The total is 117,000. The navy is divided in this way: units for NATO, Korean force and defence of coastal waters, 7,600; training staffs and trainees, 6,900; commands and administration, 1,600; dockyards and bases, 2,700; total, 18,800.
The army: units for NATO, Korean force and defence of Canada, 28,000; training staffs and trainees, 8,000; commands and administration, 2,900; service units, 10,500; total, 49,400.
The air force: units for NATO and the defence of Canada, 16,800; air transport, search and rescue, 4,400; training staffs and trainees, 21,000; commands and administration, 2,100; service units, 4,500; total, 48,800; grand total, 117,000.

If I may supplement the question the hon. member for York West has asked, it seems to me the minister's answers today show some advance with respect to the Long Branch situation. As I recall the answers I received last year to the same questions, an effort was being made to find an alternative rifle range in the vicinity of Toronto but not so far away as Camp Borden. May I take it that now the department has decided that Camp Borden will be used instead of Long Branch, and the department have given up the search for an alternative and have settled on Camp Borden as the new site for the rifle ranges which were at Long Branch?

Yes. We spent considerable time searching without success for a suitable site nearer to Toronto. I suppose we could be searching yet, but I decided that we had


covered the field and that something should be done about the matter. We are now committed to Camp Borden.

In connection with the item for aircraft and engines on page 319, which is also referred to on page 42 of the white paper in paragraph 157, can the minister tell us how many airplanes were acquired for the navy last year, whether they were purchased in Canada, whether the engines listed were purchased in Canada, and if they were not purchased in Canada, was any attempt made to obtain suitable aircraft in Canada?

We always try to procure aircraft and engines in Canada if we can find suitable ones for the purpose for which we are acquiring them, and we go outside Canada only when we feel that it is not reasonably possible to obtain them here.
I think it has not been the practice, and I am sure it should not be, to give out the numbers of planes acquired for the services.
Were these planes acquired in Canada, or were they purchased outside?

I understand that planes
for the navy are being manufactured in Canada, but we did purchase a number of helicopters outside of Canada.
Were the motors manufactured in Canada?
The question of manufacturing engines for aircraft in Canada is being considered by the Department of Defence Production, and that department has not decided whether they will be made in Canada.
What company is manufacturing the planes?
The de Havilland company.

During the general discussion yesterday I mentioned the merchant aircraft carrier which was used for escort work during the last war. Would the minister comment as to whether the construction of aircraft carriers of that type has been considered by the department and, if so, why has it been decided not to go into the construction of that type of ship?

I understand that any consideration that was being given to the proposal mentioned by the hon. member has been suspended for the time being. Studies as to the usefulness and acceptability of helicopters are now engaging our attention.

At the top of page 319 is an item covering films, displays, broadcasting,

advertising, and other informational materials, $316,000. Can the minister tell us how much money was spent on advertising, which I presume would be for recruiting purposes?

Practically the whole of
this vote will be for recruiting advertising in one way or another. The largest item is advertising in publications, $123,000, and then there is an item of $25,000 for radio advertising. Another item which may be only indirectly related to recruiting advertising is the cost of exhibition displays, which runs to $23,000. Then there is an item of $60,000 for a mobile recruiting unit. All the expenditures under this item are directly or indirectly connected with recruiting.

Has consideration been given to greatly reducing this expenditure on newspaper advertising in connection with recruiting? In my general remarks on these estimates I pointed out that it was my feeling, which is shared by a large number of other people with whom I have discussed the matter, that ads in newspapers and periodicals to join the navy and see the world, so to speak, are largely ineffective. A great number of the persons joining the navy would do so without this advertising. It is my contention that many of these ads are never looked at. If a person is really interested in joining the navy, and many are, he can find out how to go about it from divisional headquarters or other recruiting centres. It is my feeling that much of this advertising reaches only the last 30 per cent of the recruits obtained. My feeling is that consideration should be given to greatly reducing this item.
The hon. member will notice that it is reduced from $360,000 to $316,000, and the total for the three services has been reduced from $2,820,000 to $2,317,000, or a reduction of $503,000.
That is a step in the right direction.

Perhaps I may be forgiven for referring again to municipal and public utility services, which item is to be found on page 319. I asked some questions previously about this item. Am I correct in assuming that there are municipalities which provide services to the department which are paid for on a tariff basis only, with no capital assistance given either directly or under the Municipal Grants Act?

I hesitate to say definitely, but I feel quite sure there are. I know that on a number of occasions we have negotiated on a straight basis of tariff rates for services to be provided and have concluded some arrangements in that regard.
Supply-National Defence

Would the minister give some thought to providing some assistance, either in the way of capital grants under this item or under the Municipal Grants Act? Obviously it means that in some cases the ordinary home owner is paying more than his proper proportion to provide these services.

I should like to correct the low opinion of the hon. member for Oxford of the value of newspaper advertising. That opinion is certainly not shared by the successful premier of Ontario, and it is certainly not shared by many of the successful businessmen who are the backbone of the support of the Conservative party. As long as there is anything to advertise, all business experience is that newspapers provide the best medium.

Does the item "Repairs and upkeep of equipment" on page 319 cover repairs to ships, or would that be under the item "ships, $73,000,000"? Does the minister's department designate where ship repairs will be carried out, or does that come under the maritime commission?

The item of $18,890,000 covering repairs and upkeep of equipment covers repairs to ships, whereas the item of $73,000,000 under the heading major procurement of equipment, ships, refers to the acquisition of new ships. In answering the second question may I say that we lay out a work plan in the navy for repairs and maintenance of ships, and then the Canadian maritime commission of the Department of Transport is charged with allocating the work. We let them know what we want done and where the ship is located and they determine, I think in the interests of keeping as many yards active as possible, where the work should be done. They are able to judge this because they are aware of what civilian work is being done as well.

We are certainly not going to finish these estimates tonight, and when they are again before the committee I wonder if the minister could give us a breakdown of the expenditures last year on repairs. Can he give us the breakdown as between the different places in Canada? Perhaps he can do it now. Can he also give us the number of jobs and where they were performed, and the breakdown showing the expenditures, up to as recent a date as possible?

I would suggest that the hon. member could more readily get this information from the maritime commission. We keep the accounts, of course, but we do not keep a running account of the amounts

Supply-National Defence paid at different locations. The maritime commission has those figures at its fingertips, and you might get them more quickly from the commission.

I am not interested in getting it at my fingertips. I suspect that the navy has a fairly accurate picture of the expenditures made on the various ships that come within the department, and I should like to ask that next week the minister give us whatever information he has. If it is not satisfactory, we can take up the question with the maritime commission.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with the big item in the naval estimates, which was $93 million last year and is $73 million this year, for the procurement of ships, could the minister tell us what proportion of those two amounts will be spent on the long-building 14 naval destroyers? We have had these 14 destroyers or destroyer escorts appearing in the estimates for a long period now. I believe it would also be very interesting to the committee to find out how much these destroyer escorts are going to cost. What is the present estimate of the total cost per destroyer escort?
I shall have to endeavour to get that information for the hon. member.
Would the minister give us the information as to where they are being built at the same time?

Mr. Chairman, on a point of privilege, in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South I thought I should like to get something quite straight in his mind and for the record. It is this. The remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South indicated to the committee that I had no knowledge of the value of advertising. I am as fully aware as the hon. member for Vancouver South of the great value of newspaper advertising for many commercial purposes, but I still seriously doubt the value of newspaper advertising in selling a commodity such as the Royal Canadian Navy. In selling furniture and various other commercial products, yes; but the Royal Canadian Navy, I am afraid, no.

The minister might feel fairly happy about what he has done today and call it a day. If there is any disposition to have this carried, Mr. Chairman, I might simply suggest that it is easy to call it ten o'clock, if the minister agrees.
It is cooler here than outside.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that I call it ten o'clock and report progress?

I do not think we should begin on the army tonight.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On Monday we shall begin with the Defence Production Act, then take the Library of Parliament Act, the resolution with respect to judges' salaries, the resolution with respect to the Criminal Code, and the committee stage of the Canada Elections Act. Then we shall take the customs resolutions.
Is it the intention to carry on with that list on Tuesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The intention is to carry on with legislation on Tuesday and Wednesday, and estimates after that.
I do not wish to extend this too much but so we may understand I should like to ask this. Since the Defence Production Act debate will not be finished on Monday, will it continue on Tuesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, we shall take the other items I mentioned.

At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
